people.name: Ptolemy (Valentinian teacher)
people.summary: Second-century Valentinian teacher whose Letter to Flora, preserved by Epiphanius, sorts the Mosaic law into parts.

entries.title: Passover
entries.subtitle: Pesach: the night of deliverance
entries.summary: The spring festival remembering the night the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt. A household meal of lamb, unleavened bread and bitter herbs that Jesus made the setting of the Last Supper.

entries.title: Feast of Unleavened Bread
entries.subtitle: Chag HaMatzot: seven days without leaven
entries.summary: The seven-day festival that follows Passover, when Israel ate only unleavened bread in memory of leaving Egypt in haste.

entries.title: Firstfruits
entries.subtitle: The first sheaf of the barley harvest
entries.summary: The waving of the first sheaf (omer) of barley before the LORD during the week of Unleavened Bread. Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of them that slept".

entries.title: Shavuot (Pentecost)
entries.subtitle: The Feast of Weeks
entries.summary: The wheat-harvest festival held fifty days after the first sheaf. In Acts 2 it is the day the Spirit was poured out on Jesus' followers in Jerusalem.

entries.title: Feast of Trumpets
entries.subtitle: Yom Teruah / Rosh Hashanah
entries.summary: A day of trumpet blasts on the first day of the seventh month, opening the autumn festival season. In later Judaism it became Rosh Hashanah, the New Year.

entries.title: Day of Atonement
entries.subtitle: Yom Kippur: the cleansing of the sanctuary
entries.summary: The one day each year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to purify the sanctuary and the people. Hebrews reads it as a picture of Christ's entry into the Father's presence.

entries.title: Feast of Tabernacles
entries.subtitle: Sukkot: booths, harvest and joy
entries.summary: The week-long autumn harvest festival when Israel lived in booths, remembering the wilderness journey. Jesus taught at this feast about living water and the light of the world.

entries.title: Sabbath
entries.subtitle: Shabbat: the seventh-day rest
entries.summary: The weekly day of rest rooted in creation and the exodus, the sign of Israel's covenant with God. Jesus called himself Lord of the Sabbath and offered rest to the weary.

entries.title: Hanukkah
entries.subtitle: The Feast of Dedication
entries.summary: The eight-day winter festival remembering the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after its desecration by Antiochus IV. Jesus was in the temple at this feast in John 10.

entries.title: Purim
entries.subtitle: The feast of lots
entries.summary: The late-winter festival celebrating the deliverance of the Jews of Persia in the book of Esther, kept with feasting, gifts and gifts to the poor.

entries.title: Burnt Offering
entries.subtitle: Olah: the offering that goes up
entries.summary: The whole offering, entirely burned on the altar as a pleasing aroma to God. It was the daily morning and evening sacrifice and the basic act of approach and self-giving.

data.portion: Everything burned on the altar except the hide, which went to the officiating priest (Lev 7:8).

entries.title: Grain Offering
entries.subtitle: Minchah: the gift
entries.summary: A bloodless offering of fine flour, oil and frankincense, or baked cakes. A token portion was burned and the rest eaten by the priests.

data.portion: A handful with the frankincense (the 'memorial') burned; the rest eaten by the priests in the holy place (Lev 2:2-3; 6:16).

entries.title: Peace Offering
entries.subtitle: Shelamim: the fellowship meal
entries.summary: The sacrifice that ended in a meal shared by God, the priests and the worshipper's household. Offered for thanksgiving, vows or as a freewill gift.

data.portion: Fat and kidneys burned to God; the breast and right thigh to the priests; the rest eaten by the worshipper, family and guests (Lev 3:3-5; 7:15-34).

entries.title: Sin (Purification) Offering
entries.subtitle: Chatat: cleansing God's dwelling
entries.summary: The offering for unintentional sins and certain impurities, whose blood was applied to the altar or sanctuary to purge defilement so that God could keep living among his people.

animals: young bull (high priest or whole congregation)
a tenth of an ephah of flour (the very poor)
data.portion: Fat burned; for an individual's offering the priests eat the meat in the holy place (Lev 6:26); when the blood was taken inside the tent the carcass was burned outside the camp (Lev 4:11-12; 6:30).

entries.title: Guilt (Reparation) Offering
entries.subtitle: Asham: making things right
entries.summary: The offering for breaches of trust against holy things or against a neighbour. Restitution plus a fifth came first; then a ram was offered.

data.portion: Fat burned on the altar; the meat eaten by the priests in the holy place (Lev 7:3-6).

entries.title: The Two Goats of the Day of Atonement
entries.subtitle: One for the LORD, one for Azazel
entries.summary: On Yom Kippur one goat was offered as a purification offering to cleanse the sanctuary; the other, the scapegoat, carried Israel's confessed sins away alive into the wilderness.

animals: a bull (for the high priest and his house)
data.portion: The LORD's goat: blood brought behind the veil, fat burned, carcass burned outside the camp (Lev 16:25, 27). The Azazel goat: not killed, but sent alive into the wilderness (Lev 16:21-22).

entries.title: The Red Heifer
entries.subtitle: Water for cleansing from death
entries.summary: A red cow burned whole outside the camp; its ashes were mixed with running water to cleanse anyone defiled by contact with a corpse.

animals: a red heifer without blemish, never yoked
data.portion: Burned whole outside the camp with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet; the ashes kept for the water of purification (Num 19:5-9).

entries.title: The Passover Lamb
entries.subtitle: A lamb for a household
entries.summary: The year-old lamb or kid killed on 14 Nisan, whose blood marked Israel's homes and whose meat was eaten in a family meal before the exodus.

animals: a male lamb or kid of the first year, without blemish (Exod 12:5)
data.portion: Roasted whole and eaten entirely by the household that night; nothing left until morning; no bone broken (Exod 12:8-10, 46).

entries.title: Moral, Civil and Ceremonial Law
entries.subtitle: How the threefold division arose
entries.summary: Christians often divide the Torah into moral, civil (judicial) and ceremonial laws. The Torah itself makes no such division; this entry traces where the scheme came from and what it helps and hides.

entries.title: The Ten Commandments
entries.subtitle: The Ten Words
entries.summary: The ten words spoken at Sinai and written on two stone tablets, opening with God's act of rescue and setting out life with God and neighbour.

entries.title: The Shema
entries.subtitle: Hear, O Israel
entries.summary: Israel's central confession: the LORD is one, and he is to be loved with all one's heart, soul and might. Jesus called it the first commandment.

entries.title: Love Your Neighbour
entries.subtitle: Leviticus 19:18
entries.summary: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." A command from the heart of Leviticus that Jesus placed second only to the Shema.

entries.title: Love the Stranger
entries.subtitle: The foreigner in Israel
entries.summary: Israel is commanded again and again to protect and love the resident foreigner, "for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt".

entries.title: The Sabbath Commandment
entries.subtitle: Keeping the seventh day holy
entries.summary: The fourth commandment and its legal applications in Israel, and Jesus' disputes about what the Sabbath is for.

entries.title: Clean and Unclean
entries.subtitle: The purity laws of Leviticus 11–15
entries.summary: Rules about ritual impurity from death, bodily discharges and skin disease. Impurity was not sin, but it had to be kept away from God's dwelling.

entries.title: Food Laws
entries.subtitle: Clean and unclean animals
entries.summary: The rules about which animals Israel could eat, a daily sign of being set apart from the nations. Jesus declared all foods clean.

entries.title: The Jubilee
entries.subtitle: The fiftieth year of release
entries.summary: Every fiftieth year land returned to its ancestral families and Israelite slaves went free. Jesus announced his ministry in jubilee language.

entries.title: The Sabbatical Year
entries.subtitle: Shemittah: rest for the land and release of debts
entries.summary: Every seventh year the land lay fallow, the poor ate its produce, and debts between Israelites were released.

entries.title: Gleaning
entries.subtitle: Leaving the edges for the poor
entries.summary: Farmers were to leave the corners of their fields, dropped grain, forgotten sheaves and the last grapes and olives for the poor, the stranger, the orphan and the widow.

entries.title: Cities of Refuge
entries.subtitle: Protection for the manslayer
entries.summary: Six cities where someone who had killed unintentionally could flee from the avenger of blood until a trial, and live until the death of the high priest.

entries.title: Eye for an Eye
entries.subtitle: The law of proportion (lex talionis)
entries.summary: "Eye for eye, tooth for tooth": a rule for judges that limited punishment to the harm done. Jesus told his followers not to use it for personal retaliation.

entries.title: The Kinsman-Redeemer
entries.subtitle: The go'el
entries.summary: The nearest relative's duty to buy back family land, free a relative sold into servitude, and protect the family line. God calls himself Israel's Redeemer.

entries.title: Creation (Adamic) Covenant
entries.subtitle: Was there a covenant with Adam?
entries.summary: Some theologians see a covenant between God and humanity in Genesis 1–3, though the word 'covenant' is not used there. Its existence and nature are debated.

data.parties: God and Adam (and through him, humanity)
data.sign: None named in the text (some suggest the tree of life or the Sabbath)
data.promise: Life, fruitfulness and dominion in communion with God (Gen 1:26-28; 2:15-17)

entries.title: Covenant with Noah
entries.subtitle: God's promise to all creation
entries.summary: After the flood God made an unconditional covenant with Noah, his descendants and every living creature, never again to destroy the earth by flood. Its sign is the rainbow.

data.parties: God with Noah, his descendants and every living creature (Gen 9:9-10)
data.promise: Never again a flood to destroy all flesh; seedtime and harvest will not cease (Gen 8:21-22; 9:11)

entries.title: Covenant with Abraham
entries.subtitle: Land, seed and blessing for the nations
entries.summary: God's promise to Abraham of descendants, land and a great name, so that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed. God alone passed between the pieces.

data.parties: God with Abram/Abraham and his seed
data.promise: A great nation, land, a great name and blessing for all the families of the earth (Gen 12:1-3; 15:5, 18; 17:4-8)

entries.title: Covenant at Sinai
entries.subtitle: The Mosaic covenant
entries.summary: The covenant God made with Israel at Sinai after the exodus, giving the Torah and calling Israel to be a kingdom of priests. It was sealed with blood and a meal on the mountain.

data.promise: Israel as God's 'peculiar treasure', a kingdom of priests and a holy nation; life and blessing in the land (Exod 19:5-6; Deut 28:1-14; 30:15-20)

entries.title: Covenant with the Priests
entries.subtitle: Levi, Aaron and Phinehas
entries.summary: God's covenant with the priestly line: a 'covenant of salt' with Aaron's house and a 'covenant of peace' with Phinehas, promising a lasting priesthood.

data.parties: God with Levi and the priestly house of Aaron, renewed with Phinehas
data.sign: No single sign; called a 'covenant of salt' (Num 18:19)

entries.title: Covenant with David
entries.subtitle: A house, a throne and a son
entries.summary: God's promise that David's line would rule for ever, with a son whom God himself would call his son. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as that king, enthroned at the resurrection.

data.parties: God with David and his house
data.sign: No ritual sign; the enduring dynasty and throne
data.promise: A house, a kingdom and a throne for ever; a son whom God will father (2 Sam 7:12-16)

entries.title: The New Covenant
entries.subtitle: The law written on the heart
entries.summary: The covenant promised by Jeremiah and Ezekiel and inaugurated by Jesus at the Last Supper: God's law on the heart, every member knowing God, sins remembered no more.

data.parties: God with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, opened to the nations in Christ
data.sign: The cup of the Lord's Supper (Luke 22:20); the gift of the Spirit
data.promise: The law within, written on the heart; 'they shall all know me'; iniquity forgiven and sin remembered no more (Jer 31:33-34)

entries.title: The Gate of the Court
entries.subtitle: The one way in, from the east
entries.summary: The single, wide entrance to the tabernacle courtyard on its east side, a screen of coloured linen.

data.material: Screen of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twined linen, 20 cubits wide, hung on four pillars (Exod 27:16)

entries.title: The Bronze Altar
entries.subtitle: The altar of burnt offering
entries.summary: The large altar just inside the gate where the sacrifices were offered, with a fire that was never to go out.

data.material: Acacia wood overlaid with bronze, 5 by 5 cubits and 3 cubits high, with a horn at each corner and a bronze grating (Exod 27:1-4)

entries.title: The Bronze Laver
entries.subtitle: The basin for washing
entries.summary: The bronze basin between the altar and the tent where the priests washed their hands and feet before serving.

data.material: Bronze, made from the mirrors of the women who served at the door of the tent (Exod 38:8); no dimensions given

entries.title: The Holy Place
entries.subtitle: The outer room of the tent
entries.summary: The first room of the tabernacle tent, where the priests served daily at the lampstand, the table and the incense altar.

data.material: Gold-overlaid acacia boards covered by curtains of fine linen woven with cherubim, then goat-hair, ram-skin and outer leather coverings (Exod 26); about 20 by 10 cubits

entries.title: The Golden Lampstand
entries.subtitle: The menorah
entries.summary: The seven-branched lampstand of pure gold, shaped like an almond tree, that lit the holy place.

data.material: Hammered from a talent of pure gold, with a central shaft, six branches and cups shaped like almond blossoms (Exod 25:31-39)

entries.title: The Table and the Bread of the Presence
entries.subtitle: Bread before God's face
entries.summary: The gold-covered table in the holy place on which twelve loaves were set out before the LORD every Sabbath.

data.material: Acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, 2 cubits long, 1 wide and 1.5 high, with a gold moulding (Exod 25:23-24)

entries.title: The Altar of Incense
entries.subtitle: The golden altar before the veil
entries.summary: The small gold-covered altar in front of the veil where incense was burned morning and evening.

data.material: Acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, 1 cubit square and 2 high, with horns and a gold crown moulding (Exod 30:1-3)

entries.title: The Veil
entries.subtitle: The curtain before the Most Holy Place
entries.summary: The curtain woven with cherubim that separated the holy place from the most holy place. At Jesus' death the temple veil was torn from top to bottom.

data.material: Blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twined linen with cherubim woven in, hung on four gold-overlaid acacia pillars (Exod 26:31-32)

entries.title: The Most Holy Place
entries.subtitle: The holy of holies
entries.summary: The inner room of the tabernacle, a perfect cube, where the ark stood and God's presence dwelt between the cherubim.

data.material: A room of gold-overlaid acacia boards under the linen curtains, about 10 cubits each way (inferred from the boards); Solomon's was 20 cubits each way, overlaid with gold (1 Kgs 6:20)

entries.title: The Ark and the Mercy Seat
entries.subtitle: The meeting place
entries.summary: The gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the covenant, with its golden cover (the kapporet) and two cherubim. Here God promised to meet with Moses.

data.material: Acacia chest overlaid with gold, 2.5 by 1.5 by 1.5 cubits; cover of pure gold with two hammered gold cherubim (Exod 25:10-20)

entries.title: The Angel of the LORD and Hagar
entries.subtitle: The God who sees
entries.summary: The first appearance of the angel of the LORD, to a runaway Egyptian slave woman, who names God "the God who sees me".

data.form: The angel of the LORD, speaking as God

entries.title: The Visitors at Mamre
entries.subtitle: The LORD at Abraham's table
entries.summary: Three men visit Abraham by the oaks of Mamre and share his meal; one of them is identified as the LORD.

data.form: A man, one of three guests (with two angels)

entries.title: The Angel at Moriah
entries.subtitle: The LORD will provide
entries.summary: The angel of the LORD stops Abraham from sacrificing Isaac and swears an oath in God's own name.

data.form: The angel of the LORD, calling from heaven

entries.title: Jacob's Wrestler
entries.subtitle: Face to face at Peniel
entries.summary: A mysterious man wrestles with Jacob through the night, blesses him and renames him Israel. Jacob says he has seen God face to face.

data.form: A man who wrestles; later called God and an angel

entries.title: The Burning Bush
entries.subtitle: I AM THAT I AM
entries.summary: The angel of the LORD appears to Moses in a flame in a bush that is not consumed, and God speaks his name.

data.form: The angel of the LORD in a flame of fire

entries.title: The Angel Who Bears the Name
entries.subtitle: "My name is in him"
entries.summary: The angel God sends ahead of Israel in the wilderness, who can forgive or withhold forgiveness because God's name is in him.

data.form: An angel going before Israel, associated with the pillar of cloud

entries.title: The Commander of the LORD's Army
entries.subtitle: Joshua at Jericho
entries.summary: Before the battle of Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who says he is the commander of the army of the LORD, and Joshua worships him.

data.form: A man with a drawn sword

entries.title: The Angel of the LORD and Gideon
entries.subtitle: "The LORD is with thee"
entries.summary: The angel of the LORD sits under an oak at Ophrah, commissions Gideon, and consumes his offering with fire. Gideon fears he will die because he has seen the angel face to face.

data.form: The angel of the LORD, sitting under an oak

entries.title: The Angel and Manoah
entries.subtitle: "Why askest thou my name, seeing it is secret?"
entries.summary: The angel of the LORD announces Samson's birth, refuses to give his name, which is 'wonderful', and ascends in the flame of the altar.

data.form: A man of God with the appearance of an angel

entries.title: The Word of the LORD Who Came
entries.subtitle: A word that stands and speaks
entries.summary: In some passages 'the word of the LORD' comes to a prophet in a way that sounds personal and even visible: to Abram in a vision, to Samuel at Shiloh, to Jeremiah with a touch.

data.form: The Word of the LORD, appearing in vision

entries.title: The Fourth Man in the Fire
entries.subtitle: "Like the Son of God"
entries.summary: When Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego are thrown into the furnace, Nebuchadnezzar sees a fourth figure walking with them, unharmed.

data.form: A fourth figure in the furnace

entries.title: Melchizedek
entries.subtitle: King of righteousness, king of peace
entries.summary: The priest-king of Salem who blesses Abram with bread and wine. Some have seen him as an appearance of Christ; most read him as a historical figure who serves as a type of Christ.

entries.title: One
entries.subtitle: Echad: unity and uniqueness
entries.summary: One expresses the uniqueness of Israel's God and the unity he creates among his people.

data.caution: 'One' (echad) can describe a united whole (one flesh, one cluster) as well as a single item. That is worth noticing, but the word alone cannot prove the Trinity, and arguments built on it alone overreach.

entries.title: Three
entries.subtitle: Completion, emphasis and the third day
entries.summary: Three marks emphasis and completion, and especially 'the third day' as the day of God's decisive action.

data.caution: Threefold patterns are common in all storytelling and speech. Not every three points to the Trinity or to the resurrection; look for clear textual links before drawing them.

entries.title: Four
entries.subtitle: The four corners of the earth
entries.summary: Four is the number of the world's directions and its whole extent: four winds, four corners, four rivers, four living creatures.

data.caution: Four usually means 'in every direction'. Arguments that something must be fourfold because the world has four corners are arguments from fittingness, not evidence.

entries.title: Six
entries.subtitle: The day of humanity
entries.summary: Humanity was created on the sixth day, and six marks the days of work. In Revelation 666 is 'the number of a man'.

data.caution: The popular idea that six means 'falling short of seven' is an interpretation, not something the Bible states. Six is also simply the number of working days.

entries.title: Seven
entries.subtitle: Completion, rest and oath
entries.summary: Seven is the most significant number in Scripture: the days of creation, the Sabbath, the festivals and the visions of Revelation.

data.caution: Seven clearly carries meaning in Scripture, but not every list of seven items or every seventh word is significant. Counting words to find hidden sevens is not a reliable method of interpretation.

entries.title: Ten
entries.subtitle: The ten words and the tithe
entries.summary: Ten appears in the Ten Commandments, the ten plagues and the tithe, often as a round, complete number.

data.caution: Ten is often a round number, as in our 'ten times'. It does not always carry a theological meaning.

entries.title: Twelve
entries.subtitle: The people of God
entries.summary: Twelve is the number of Israel's tribes and of Jesus' apostles, and it shapes the New Jerusalem.

data.caution: Twelve signals 'the whole people of God', but it should not be used to calculate dates or to make every group of twelve into a prophecy.

entries.title: Forty
entries.subtitle: Testing and transition
entries.summary: Forty marks periods of testing, preparation and transition: the flood, Moses on the mountain, Israel in the wilderness, Jesus in the desert.

data.caution: Forty is often a round number for 'a long time' or 'a generation'. It is a theme, not a calendar, and should not be used to set dates.

entries.title: Seventy
entries.subtitle: The nations and the fullness of time
entries.summary: Seventy is linked to the nations of the world, Israel's elders, the exile and Daniel's seventy weeks.

data.caution: Seventy is often a round number, and the count of nations in Genesis 10 depends on how one counts. Daniel's seventy weeks have been used for countless failed date-setting schemes.

entries.subtitle: The sealed servants of God
entries.summary: Revelation numbers the sealed servants of God at 144,000, twelve thousand from each tribe, and then shows a multitude no one could number.

data.caution: Reading 144,000 as an exact headcount, or as a special class separate from other believers, ignores Revelation's symbolic use of numbers and the vision of the countless multitude that follows.

entries.subtitle: The number of the beast
entries.summary: "Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six" (Rev 13:18).

data.caution: Every generation has found a candidate for 666, from emperors and popes to modern politicians and technologies. The original readers were expected to calculate it, which points to their own time.

entries.subtitle: The thousand years
entries.summary: A thousand is the number of fullness and vast extent, and Revelation 20 speaks of Christ's saints reigning for a thousand years.

data.caution: Most biblical uses of 'thousand' are clearly not literal counts (a thousand hills, a thousand generations). Whether the millennium of Revelation 20 is a literal period is one of the most debated questions in eschatology.

entries.title: Adam and Christ
entries.subtitle: The first and the last Adam
entries.summary: Paul calls Adam 'the figure of him that was to come'. Where the first Adam brought death, the last Adam brings life.

data.type: Adam, the first human and son of God
data.antitype: Christ, the last Adam and head of a new humanity

entries.title: Isaac and Christ
entries.subtitle: The beloved son offered
entries.summary: Abraham's offering of Isaac, his only beloved son, on Moriah foreshadows the Father's giving of his Son, though God stops Abraham's hand and provides the sacrifice himself.

data.type: Isaac, Abraham's beloved son, bound on Moriah
data.antitype: Christ, the Father's beloved Son, given for the world

entries.title: Joseph and Christ
entries.subtitle: The rejected brother who saves
entries.summary: Joseph, the beloved son rejected by his brothers, sold, and then exalted to save many lives, is a pattern many readers see fulfilled in Jesus.

data.type: Joseph, beloved son, rejected and exalted
data.antitype: Christ, rejected by his own and exalted to give life

entries.title: Moses and Christ
entries.subtitle: The prophet like Moses
entries.summary: Moses promised a prophet like himself. The New Testament presents Jesus as that prophet, and greater: Moses was a servant in God's house, Jesus is the Son over it.

data.antitype: Christ, the prophet like Moses and the Son over God's house

entries.title: The Passover Lamb and Christ
entries.subtitle: The Lamb who conquers
entries.summary: The Passover lamb whose blood marked Israel's homes for deliverance becomes the Lamb of God, slain yet standing on the throne.

data.type: The Passover lamb of the exodus
data.antitype: Christ, the Lamb of God who sets his people free

entries.title: Manna and the Bread of Life
entries.subtitle: Bread from heaven
entries.summary: God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness. Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven that gives life to the world.

data.type: Manna, the daily bread from heaven
data.antitype: Christ, the living bread who gives life to the world

entries.title: The Rock in the Wilderness
entries.subtitle: "That Rock was Christ"
entries.summary: Water flowed from the rock struck by Moses in the wilderness. Paul says, 'they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.'

data.type: The rock that gave water in the wilderness
data.antitype: Christ, the source of living water

entries.title: The Bronze Serpent
entries.subtitle: Lifted up to give life
entries.summary: Moses lifted a bronze serpent on a pole so that those bitten could look and live. Jesus said the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way.

data.type: The bronze serpent lifted on a pole
data.antitype: Christ lifted up on the cross

entries.title: Jonah and Christ
entries.subtitle: The sign of Jonah
entries.summary: Jesus said the only sign given to his generation would be the sign of Jonah: three days in the heart of the earth, and a call to repentance that reaches the nations.

data.type: Jonah, three days in the fish and a preacher to Nineveh
data.antitype: Christ, three days in the grave and raised, preached to the nations

entries.title: David and Christ
entries.subtitle: The shepherd king
entries.summary: David, the anointed shepherd-king who defeats Israel's enemy and receives the promise of an eternal throne, is the pattern for the Messiah, the Son of David.

data.type: David, anointed shepherd-king and champion of Israel
data.antitype: Christ, the Son of David, shepherd and conquering king

entries.title: Melchizedek and Christ
entries.subtitle: A priest for ever
entries.summary: Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem, is the pattern Hebrews uses for Christ's eternal priesthood, which does not depend on descent from Levi.

data.type: Melchizedek, priest of God Most High and king of Salem
data.antitype: Christ, eternal priest-king after the order of Melchizedek

entries.title: The Tabernacle and Christ
entries.subtitle: God pitching his tent among us
entries.summary: The tabernacle was God's dwelling among his people. John says the Word 'dwelt' (pitched his tent) among us, and Revelation ends with God's tabernacle with humanity.

data.type: The tabernacle, God's portable dwelling in Israel's camp
data.antitype: Christ, God dwelling in human flesh; and the church and new creation as his dwelling

entries.title: The Day of Atonement and Christ
entries.subtitle: The high priest who enters once for all
entries.summary: Hebrews reads the yearly entry of the high priest into the Most Holy Place as a pattern of Christ's entry into the Father's presence with his own blood.

data.type: The high priest's yearly entry behind the veil
data.antitype: Christ's once-for-all entry into heaven itself, opening the way for us

entries.title: Exodus and New Exodus
entries.subtitle: The pattern of liberation
entries.summary: The exodus from Egypt became the template for God's future rescue. The prophets promised a new exodus, and the Gospels present Jesus as leading it.

data.antitype: Christ's death and resurrection, the new exodus from sin and death

entries.title: Temple and Body
entries.subtitle: "Destroy this temple"
entries.summary: Jesus spoke of his own body as the temple. The New Testament then calls the church, and the believer's body, God's temple by the Spirit.

data.type: The Jerusalem temple, God's house among his people
data.antitype: Christ's risen body, and his people as the temple of the Spirit

entries.title: Sabbath and Rest
entries.subtitle: Entering God's rest
entries.summary: The Sabbath rest of creation and the promised rest of the land point to the rest Christ gives, a share in God's own rest.

data.type: The Sabbath and the rest of the promised land
data.antitype: The rest of God's people in Christ, now and in the new creation

entries.title: The Flood Narrative
entries.subtitle: A palistrophe turning on 'God remembered Noah'
entries.summary: The flood story in Genesis 6–9 is arranged as a large mirror pattern: numbers and events rise to the high point of the waters and then fall away in reverse order, with 'God remembered Noah' at the centre.

levels.label: A
levels.text: Noah and his three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth

levels.label: B
levels.text: God will establish his covenant with Noah

levels.label: C
levels.text: Seven days until the rain
