blocks.subject: entry:festival/passover
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Passover begins in Exod 12. Each household chooses a year-old male lamb or kid on the 10th of the first month (Nisan, also called Abib), keeps it until the 14th and kills it "between the evenings" (at twilight). Its blood is put on the doorposts and lintel with hyssop, and the meat is roasted and eaten that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, by people dressed for a journey (Exod 12:3-11).

The blood is called a **sign** for Israel: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you" (Exod 12:13). The same night God judges "all the gods of Egypt" (Exod 12:12) and frees the people Pharaoh had enslaved. God had already named Israel "my son, even my firstborn" (Exod 4:22-23).

Passover is a memorial to be kept "for ever" (Exod 12:14), and it is built around children's questions (Exod 12:26-27; 13:8). Deuteronomy moves the sacrifice to the place God chooses (Deut 16:5-6), and later reforms under Hezekiah and Josiah restore it (2 Chr 30; 35).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/passover
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple period.** On the afternoon of 14 Nisan the lambs were slaughtered in the temple courts by the worshippers themselves, while priests caught and passed along the blood and the Levites sang the Hallel (Ps 113–118). The Mishnah describes the slaughter taking place in three successive groups (Mishnah Pesachim 5). The meat was then eaten that evening in Jerusalem by registered companies. Josephus gives a very large count of lambs for one Passover before the war with Rome (Jewish War 6.9.3), which shows the scale of the pilgrimage, even if the figure is rounded.

**The meal.** Mishnah Pesachim 10 describes the evening: four cups of wine, the son's questions, the retelling that begins with disgrace and ends with praise, and the Hallel split before and after the meal. It says each generation must regard itself as if it had personally come out of Egypt (Pesachim 10:5).

**Modern practice.** Since the temple's destruction in AD 70 no lamb is sacrificed. Jewish families keep the *Seder* with the Haggadah; a roasted bone on the Seder plate recalls the lamb, alongside matzah, bitter herbs, the four cups, the four questions and Elijah's cup.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/passover
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus chose Passover to explain his death. At the meal he took the bread and cup and said, in effect, *this is me, given for you* (Luke 22:15-20). Paul can say simply, "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7), and John has Jesus die at the hour the lambs were being killed, with no bone broken (John 19:14, 36; Exod 12:46).

Read on its own terms, the first Passover is a rescue story. The blood marks the households God is protecting on the night he breaks the power of Pharaoh and his gods. It is a sign of belonging, not a payment to God. The Father is bringing his firstborn son out of slavery "unto myself" (Exod 19:4).

That is why Passover fits a **Christus Victor** reading of the cross: the Lamb's death is God's victory over the powers that enslave his children, and the meal is a family meal where the freed sit down together. "Let us keep the feast" (1 Cor 5:8).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/passover
blocks.title: Melito of Sardis: the model and the reality
blocks.body: Melito's Easter homily treats the Passover as a *model* or sketch: valuable until the real thing arrives, then surpassed by it, the way an artist's preliminary model gives way to the finished work. For Melito the lamb, the blood and the exodus were the outline, and Christ's death and resurrection are the reality.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/unleavened-bread
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
From the 15th to the 21st of the first month no leaven may be eaten or even found in Israel's houses (Exod 12:15-20; Lev 23:6-8). The first and seventh days are days of holy assembly without ordinary work.

The bread is called "the bread of affliction" because Israel left Egypt "in haste" (Deut 16:3), with no time for dough to rise (Exod 12:34, 39). It is one of the three pilgrim festivals at which every male was to appear before the LORD (Deut 16:16). In the Gospels Passover and Unleavened Bread are often spoken of as one feast (Luke 22:1).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/unleavened-bread
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple period.** The Mishnah opens its tractate on Passover with the search for leaven by lamplight on the night of the 14th (Mishnah Pesachim 1:1); any found was destroyed before the festival began.

**Modern practice.** Jewish homes are cleaned of *chametz* (leavened products) beforehand, with a ceremonial search the night before Passover. Matzah is eaten through the week, and the last day is again a festival day.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/unleavened-bread
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Paul joins the two feasts: because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the church now lives the week of unleavened bread, "not with old leaven... but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 5:7-8). Removing leaven pictures a household cleared of what puffs up and spoils a shared life.

The image is flexible. Jesus warns about "the leaven of the Pharisees" (Matt 16:6), yet also likens the kingdom of heaven to leaven that works through the whole lump (Matt 13:33). Leaven is not evil in itself; the point is what is being spread through the family. The feast that began with haste out of slavery becomes a picture of a freed people learning to live together in truth.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/firstfruits
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
When Israel reaps its harvest in the land, the first sheaf (*omer*) is brought to the priest, who waves it before the LORD "on the morrow after the sabbath" (Lev 23:11). A year-old lamb is offered with it, and no new grain may be eaten until this is done (Lev 23:12-14).

The principle is that the first and best belongs to God and stands for the whole harvest (compare Exod 23:19; Deut 26:1-11). The fifty days to Shavuot are counted from this day (Lev 23:15-16).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/firstfruits
blocks.title: When was the sheaf waved?
blocks.body:
**Which "sabbath"?** Lev 23:11 does not say which sabbath it means, and Second Temple groups disagreed.

- The Pharisaic and later rabbinic view took "sabbath" to mean the first festival day of Unleavened Bread (15 Nisan), so the sheaf was waved on 16 Nisan. Josephus gives this date (Antiquities 3.10.5).
- Others, whom the Mishnah calls Boethusians (associated with the Sadducees), held that it meant the weekly Sabbath, so the sheaf was always waved on a Sunday (Mishnah Menachot 10:3).

The Mishnah also describes the public reaping of the sheaf on the evening before, with townspeople gathered round (Menachot 10:3). The date in this app follows the rabbinic reckoning.

**Modern practice.** With no temple, Jews mark the day by beginning the *counting of the omer*, a nightly count of the 49 days to Shavuot.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/firstfruits
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
"Now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Cor 15:20). The first sheaf is not a separate crop; it is the beginning of the harvest and the pledge that the rest is coming. Jesus' resurrection is the first piece of the new creation, and his people's resurrection is the rest of the same harvest (1 Cor 15:23).

On either reckoning of the date, the sheaf was waved in the days after Passover, and the Gospels place the resurrection on the first day of the week after the Passover sabbath. Paul extends the image: believers have "the firstfruits of the Spirit" while they wait for "the adoption" (Rom 8:23), and James calls the church "a kind of firstfruits of his creatures" (Jas 1:18). The Father's harvest is the whole creation brought back to life.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/shavuot
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Israel counts seven full weeks from the waving of the first sheaf, "even unto the morrow after the seventh sabbath shall ye number fifty days" (Lev 23:16). Greek-speaking Jews therefore called it *Pentecost*, "fiftieth". It is the "feast of harvest" or "feast of weeks" (Exod 23:16; 34:22) and the second of the three pilgrim feasts (Deut 16:16).

Two features stand out. The two wave loaves are baked **with leaven** (Lev 23:17), unlike almost every other grain offering. And the gleaning law is restated right in the middle of the festival calendar (Lev 23:22): the harvest feast includes the poor and the stranger. Deuteronomy tells Israel to rejoice "thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy manservant, and thy maidservant, and the Levite... and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow" (Deut 16:11).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/shavuot
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple period.** Pilgrims came to Jerusalem from across the diaspora, as the list of nations in Acts 2:9-11 shows. The Mishnah treats Shavuot as the start of the season for bringing firstfruits of the seven species to the temple and describes their procession to Jerusalem (Mishnah Bikkurim 1 and 3).

**Link to Sinai.** Israel reached Sinai "in the third month" (Exod 19:1), and rabbinic tradition came to celebrate Shavuot as the anniversary of the giving of the Torah; the Babylonian Talmud discusses whether it was given on the 6th or 7th of Sivan (Shabbat 86b).

**Modern practice.** Synagogues read the book of Ruth (set at harvest time) and the Ten Commandments; many keep an all-night study vigil, and dairy foods are customary.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/shavuot
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
On the day of Pentecost, with pilgrims from many nations in the city, the Spirit came with wind and fire (Acts 2:1-4). The scene echoes Sinai, where God came down in fire and sound (Exod 19:16-19), but now the word is written on hearts rather than stone (Jer 31:33; 2 Cor 3:3). Peter explains it as the risen Jesus, exalted to the Father's right hand, pouring out the promised Spirit (Acts 2:33).

The Spirit given is "the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Pentecost is the harvest feast in which the Father begins gathering his family from every nation, and the many languages are not erased but each hears "in our own tongue" (Acts 2:8).

Preachers often note that about three thousand died after the golden calf at Sinai (Exod 32:28) while about three thousand were added at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), and that the two leavened loaves can picture Jew and Gentile offered together. These are devotional connections, not claims the texts make.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/trumpets
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
The Torah says little about this day: "a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation", with rest from work and offerings (Lev 23:24-25; Num 29:1-6). *Teruah* means a shout or blast, used for alarms, war cries and joyful acclamation of a king (Num 10:9; 1 Sam 10:24 uses the related verb of shouting for the king).

It opens the seventh month, which also holds the Day of Atonement (10th) and Tabernacles (15th). On this date Ezra read the Torah to the returned exiles, who wept until they were told, "the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:2, 9-10).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/trumpets
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple and Mishnah.** The Mishnah names this day as one of the "new years" of the Jewish calendar (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1) and gives rules for the shofar, the ram's horn, and its blasts (Rosh Hashanah 3–4).

**Modern practice.** Rosh Hashanah is kept for two days. The shofar is sounded in the synagogue; apples dipped in honey express hope for a sweet year; and the day begins the Ten Days of Awe, a season of repentance that leads to Yom Kippur. The custom of *tashlich*, casting crumbs into flowing water while reciting Micah 7:19, is medieval.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/trumpets
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
In the New Testament the trumpet announces a King gathering his family. The Son of Man sends his angels "with a great sound of a trumpet" to gather his elect from the four winds (Matt 24:31); at "the last trump" the dead are raised incorruptible (1 Cor 15:52); and the Lord descends "with the trump of God" (1 Thess 4:16). Interpreters differ on how much of Matt 24 refers to the events of the first century; partial-preterist readers take the gathering in Matt 24:31 as the worldwide mission that followed AD 70, while 1 Cor 15 and 1 Thess 4 look to the final resurrection.

The trumpet is good news more than alarm. In Leviticus the great trumpet of the Jubilee is blown on the Day of Atonement to proclaim liberty (Lev 25:9-10). The trumpets of God call captives home and announce that the rightful King has come. Detailed end-time timetables built on this feast are speculation rather than exegesis.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/day-of-atonement
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Lev 16 sets out the day. The high priest, in plain linen, offers a bull for himself and his house. Two goats are chosen by lot: one "for the LORD" as a purification (sin) offering, one "for Azazel". The high priest takes the blood of the bull and of the LORD's goat behind the veil and sprinkles it on and before the mercy seat, and then on the altar, to "make an atonement for the holy place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel" (Lev 16:16-19).

Then he lays **both hands** on the live goat, confesses over it "all the iniquities of the children of Israel", and sends it away into the wilderness (Lev 16:21-22). The people are to "afflict your souls" (understood as fasting) and do no work (Lev 16:29-31; 23:27-32). The result: "that ye may be clean from all your sins before the LORD" (Lev 16:30).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/day-of-atonement
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple period.** The Mishnah tractate Yoma describes the day in detail: the high priest's week of preparation and night vigil, the drawing of lots, his confessions, the pronouncing of the divine Name, the entry with incense, and the leading of the goat to a cliff in the wilderness (Mishnah Yoma 3–6).

**After AD 70.** Without a temple, rabbinic Judaism held that repentance, prayer and the day itself bring atonement. Yom Kippur is kept with a 25-hour fast, confession of sin in the plural ("we have sinned"), the *Kol Nidre* service on the evening before (a medieval addition), and the reading of Jonah in the afternoon.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/day-of-atonement
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Hebrews reads the day through Jesus. He is the high priest who entered "not without blood", but by "his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption" (Heb 9:7, 12). What his blood does is **cleanse**: it will "purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (Heb 9:14). The aim of the whole ritual was that God could go on dwelling among an unclean people; the aim in Christ is that we can "draw near" into the Father's presence (Heb 10:19-22).

At Jesus' death the temple veil was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). The way in is now open, not because an angry God was appeased, but because the Son has carried our humanity, cleansed, into the Father's house.

See also the entries on the two goats (sacrifice) and the Day of Atonement typology.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/tabernacles
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
From the 15th of the seventh month Israel lives for seven days in booths of branches, "that your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt" (Lev 23:42-43). An eighth day of solemn assembly follows (Lev 23:36). It is the "feast of ingathering" at the end of the agricultural year (Exod 23:16) and the most joyful of the feasts: "thou shalt surely rejoice" (Deut 16:15).

The offerings are unusual: thirteen bulls on the first day, twelve on the second, down to seven on the seventh, **seventy** in all (Num 29:12-34). Every seventh year the Torah was read aloud to all Israel at this feast (Deut 31:10-13), and the returned exiles rediscovered the booths in Nehemiah's day (Neh 8:13-18). Zechariah foresees the nations going up to Jerusalem to keep it (Zech 14:16).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/tabernacles
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple period.** The Mishnah describes the waving of the *lulav* (palm, myrtle and willow) with the *etrog* (citron) (Mishnah Sukkah 3), a daily water libation poured at the altar from a golden flask filled at the Pool of Siloam (Sukkah 4:9), and the nightly "rejoicing of the place of water-drawing", when great golden lamps lit the Court of the Women and the pious danced with torches (Sukkah 5:1-4). The Talmud connects the seventy bulls with the seventy nations of the world (Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 55b). Josephus tells of worshippers pelting the king-priest Alexander Jannaeus with citrons during the feast (Antiquities 13.13.5).

**Modern practice.** Families build a *sukkah* and eat (sometimes sleep) in it, wave the lulav and etrog, and end with *Simchat Torah*, which completes and restarts the annual reading of the Torah.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/tabernacles
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
John sets Jesus' boldest words at this feast. "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink" (John 7:37), with water-pouring going on around him. Soon after he says, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12), in a temple known at this feast for its great lamps. And John's prologue already said the Word "dwelt" among us, literally *pitched his tent* (John 1:14).

Tabernacles celebrates God living with his people on the journey and the joy of a full harvest. In Christ, God has pitched his tent in our flesh and pours out the Spirit like rivers of living water (John 7:38-39). Zechariah's picture of the nations coming to keep the feast (Zech 14:16) fits the hope of a growing kingdom: the Father's harvest of the nations, gathered with joy (Rev 7:9-10, where the multitude hold palm branches).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/sabbath
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
On the seventh day God "rested" and "blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it" (Gen 2:2-3). The command to keep it is given two reasons. In Exodus it imitates God's own rest after creation (Exod 20:11). In Deuteronomy it remembers slavery: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt" (Deut 5:15), and it gives rest to servants, foreigners and animals too (Deut 5:14).

It is the "sign" of the covenant between God and Israel (Exod 31:13-17). The prophets call it "a delight" (Isa 58:13). It is also the one festival that is not tied to the harvest or the moon.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/sabbath
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple period.** Synagogue reading and teaching on the Sabbath were customary (Luke 4:16; Acts 15:21). The Mishnah lists thirty-nine main categories of forbidden work (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2), and the tractate Eruvin deals with the limits of movement on the day. Jesus' disputes with the Pharisees (Mark 2:23–3:6) belong to this world of careful debate about what counts as work.

**Modern practice.** Shabbat runs from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday. It opens with candle-lighting and *Kiddush* (blessing over wine) at a family meal and closes with *Havdalah*. Most Christians gather on Sunday, the day of resurrection (Acts 20:7; Rev 1:10), which some traditions treat as the Christian Sabbath and others as the Lord's Day distinct from the Sabbath.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/sabbath
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus said, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath: therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath" (Mark 2:27-28). His Sabbath healings are acts of release: a daughter of Abraham bound for eighteen years should be "loosed from this bond on the sabbath day" (Luke 13:16). He presents himself as the rest the Sabbath pointed to: "Come unto me... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

Hebrews speaks of a "sabbath rest" (*sabbatismos*) that remains for God's people, entered by trust (Heb 4:9-10), and Paul calls Sabbaths "a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ" (Col 2:16-17). The deepest Sabbath is not a day off from God but a share in the Father's own rest and delight in his finished work, given to sons and daughters rather than earned by servants.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/hanukkah
blocks.title: Historical basis
blocks.body:
Hanukkah is not commanded in the Hebrew Bible. In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes banned Jewish practice and set up an idolatrous altar in the temple, "the abomination of desolation" (1 Macc 1:54; compare Dan 11:31). After the Maccabean revolt, Judas Maccabeus and his brothers cleansed the sanctuary, built a new altar and rededicated it on 25 Kislev (164 BC), with eight days of celebration, and decreed that the days be kept every year (1 Macc 4:52-59). 2 Maccabees says the eight days were kept in the manner of Tabernacles (2 Macc 10:6).

*Hanukkah* means "dedication". Kislev is the ninth month counting from Nisan, so the festival runs from 25 Kislev into the start of Tevet.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/hanukkah
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Second Temple period.** Josephus says the festival was called "Lights" (Antiquities 12.7.7). The Mishnah mentions the Hanukkah lamp only in passing (Mishnah Bava Kamma 6:6). The well-known story of a single jar of oil that burned for eight days first appears in the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 21b), centuries later; it is not in 1 or 2 Maccabees.

**Modern practice.** Families light a nine-branched lamp (*hanukkiah*), adding one light each night, using the ninth "servant" light (*shamash*) to kindle the others. Foods fried in oil, such as latkes and doughnuts, and the spinning top (*dreidel*) are customary.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/hanukkah
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch" (John 10:22-23). At the feast of the temple's consecration, Jesus calls himself the one "whom the Father hath sanctified [consecrated], and sent into the world" (John 10:36), and says, "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30).

The Maccabees cleansed a building by force of arms. Jesus is the consecrated temple himself (John 2:19-21), the place where the Father is present, and his victory over the powers that defile God's house comes not by the sword but by the cross. Hanukkah's lights fit the One who said, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12).

blocks.subject: entry:festival/purim
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Purim comes from the book of Esther. Haman cast *pur*, "the lot", to choose the day for destroying the Jews (Esth 3:7; 9:24-26). Through Esther and Mordecai the day was "turned to the contrary" (Esth 9:1), and the Jews kept the 14th of Adar (and in Susa the 15th) as "days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor" (Esth 9:17-22).

Like Hanukkah, it is a festival established after the Torah. 2 Maccabees calls 14 Adar "Mordecai's day" (2 Macc 15:36). The name of God does not appear anywhere in the Hebrew text of Esther.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/purim
blocks.title: Second Temple and modern practice
blocks.body:
**Mishnah.** The tractate Megillah is about reading the scroll of Esther; it sets the reading on the 14th of Adar for most towns and the 15th for cities walled since the days of Joshua (Mishnah Megillah 1:1).

**Modern practice.** The scroll (*megillah*) is read publicly, with noise-making at every mention of Haman. People give food parcels to friends (*mishloach manot*) and gifts to the poor, hold a festive meal, and often wear costumes. Jerusalem keeps "Shushan Purim" on the 15th.

blocks.subject: entry:festival/purim
blocks.title: A Christian reading
blocks.body:
The New Testament never mentions Purim by name. (Some have suggested the unnamed feast of John 5:1 was Purim, but this is uncertain.) The Christian reading here is a lens, not a claim that Esther predicts Christ.

Esther shows a pattern that the cross completes: the instrument prepared to destroy the righteous becomes the defeat of the enemy. Haman was hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai (Esth 7:10). At the cross the powers did their worst and were themselves disarmed: God "made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:15). And in a book where God is never named, the Father is still at work, as Mordecai suspected: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esth 4:14).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/burnt-offering
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Lev 1).** The worshipper brings an unblemished male from the herd or flock, or birds if poor (Lev 1:3, 10, 14). At the entrance of the tent he lays his hand on its head, "and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him" (Lev 1:4). **The worshipper himself kills it**, on the north side of the altar (Lev 1:5, 11). The priests dash the blood around the altar, the animal is skinned and cut up, the entrails and legs are washed, and the whole is burned: "a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD" (Lev 1:9).

**Regular use.** A lamb was offered every morning and evening as the continual burnt offering (*tamid*) (Exod 29:38-42; Num 28:3-8), and the altar fire was never to go out (Lev 6:12-13). Burnt offerings also accompanied festivals, vows and the completion of purification. The Mishnah tractate Tamid describes the daily service in the temple.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/burnt-offering
blocks.title: Meaning: approach and self-giving
blocks.body:
*Olah* means "that which goes up": the whole animal rises to God as smoke. It is the oldest sacrifice in Scripture (Noah, Gen 8:20; Abraham, Gen 22:2), and Lev 1 does not tie it to any particular sin. Its key phrase is "a sweet savour unto the LORD": the gift is received and the worshipper accepted (Lev 1:4, 9).

The offering expresses approach, surrender and dedication. Nothing is kept back. The fire on the altar is associated with God's own presence; at the inauguration of the tabernacle "there came a fire out from before the LORD, and consumed upon the altar the burnt offering" (Lev 9:24), and the people shouted for joy.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/burnt-offering
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
The burnt offering is a gift, wholly given. That is the language the New Testament uses for the cross: Christ "hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour" (Eph 5:2). What pleases the Father is not the death as such but the Son's whole-hearted love and obedience, "who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God" (Heb 9:14).

The fire is not punishment; it is the meeting of the gift with God's presence. Believers are invited into the same self-giving: "present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God" (Rom 12:1). The Son's offering of himself to the Father becomes the shape of our own life in him.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/burnt-offering
blocks.title: How the penal reading arose
blocks.body:
In much Western preaching since the Reformation, every sacrifice is read through one lens: the animal stands in the sinner's place and is put to death as the penalty the sinner deserved. The hand-laying (Lev 1:4) is read as transferring guilt, and the slaughter as an execution.

This reading has roots in Anselm's argument that sin must be met with either satisfaction or punishment (*Cur Deus Homo* 1.11–15), though Anselm himself chose satisfaction, not punishment. The Reformers moved to a penal account: Calvin describes Christ as standing in the place of the guilty and bearing the judgment due to them (*Institutes* 2.16.5–6), and nineteenth-century Reformed theology, notably Charles Hodge, read the Levitical sacrifices as vicarious punishment.

**Why the relational reading differs.** In Lev 1 the worshipper, not the priest, kills the animal, and the killing is not described as a judicial act. No word of wrath appears in Lev 1–7; the result is "a sweet savour". The single hand laid on the burnt offering more naturally signals ownership and identification (*this is mine, offered for me*). The one place where Leviticus describes sins being placed on an animal is the two-handed confession over the scapegoat (Lev 16:21), and that goat is not killed.

citations.ref: Systematic Theology, vol. 2, on the satisfaction of Christ

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/grain-offering
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Lev 2; 6:14-23).** The worshipper brings fine flour with oil and frankincense, or unleavened cakes baked in an oven, on a griddle or in a pan, or roasted heads of new grain (Lev 2:1-14). The priest burns a handful, the "memorial" (*azkarah*), with all the frankincense; the rest is "most holy" and belongs to the priests (Lev 2:2-3, 10).

No leaven or honey may be burned on the altar, and every grain offering must be salted with "the salt of the covenant of thy God" (Lev 2:11-13). Grain and drink offerings accompanied burnt and peace offerings (Num 15:1-16).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/grain-offering
blocks.title: Meaning: gift and covenant table
blocks.body:
*Minchah* is the ordinary Hebrew word for a gift or tribute: Jacob's present to Esau (Gen 32:13), the tribute of subject kings (2 Sam 8:2), and the offerings of Cain and Abel (Gen 4:3-5). In Leviticus it becomes the name of the grain offering.

It involves **no blood and no death**. It is the fruit of the worshipper's labour given back to God, with salt marking covenant loyalty. Most of it is eaten by the priests, so it is also a meal shared within God's household. A poor person could even bring flour as a purification offering (Lev 5:11-13).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/grain-offering
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
The grain offering is a reminder that Israel's worship was not mainly about killing. It is a gift from a son to a father, the work of one's hands brought to the table.

Christians have long seen in it the Lord's Supper, where bread is offered with thanksgiving and shared. Jesus calls himself "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and the church's meal is a covenant table where the Father feeds his children.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/grain-offering
blocks.title: Justin Martyr: the flour offering and the Eucharist
blocks.body: Justin argues that the offering of fine flour presented for those cleansed of skin disease was a figure of the bread of the Eucharist, and that Malachi's prophecy of a pure offering among the Gentiles (Mal 1:11) refers to the bread and cup Christians offer in thanksgiving.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/grain-offering
blocks.title: Why the penal reading struggles here
blocks.body:
Penal accounts of sacrifice, which treat every offering as a death in the sinner's place, usually pass over the grain offering. But it stands among the five main offerings of Lev 1–7, and flour could even serve as a purification offering for the poor (Lev 5:11-13).

That a bloodless gift can "make atonement" in Leviticus (Lev 5:13) shows that the system did not rest on the idea that a death penalty must be paid. Atonement in Leviticus is broader: cleansing, reparation and restored fellowship.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/peace-offering
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Lev 3; 7:11-36).** The worshipper lays a hand on the animal and kills it at the tent; the priests dash the blood on the altar. The fat covering the entrails and the kidneys are burned: "all the fat is the LORD's" (Lev 3:16). The breast is waved before the LORD and given to the priests, with the right thigh (Lev 7:30-34). The rest of the meat is eaten by the worshipper and those invited, in a state of ritual purity (Lev 7:19-21).

There are three kinds (Lev 7:12-16): the **thanksgiving** offering (*todah*), eaten the same day with leavened and unleavened bread; the **vow** offering; and the **freewill** offering.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/peace-offering
blocks.title: Meaning: communion
blocks.body:
The name is related to *shalom*, peace and wholeness. This is the only offering in which the worshipper eats. God receives the choicest part, the priests receive their share, and the family feasts "before the LORD thy God... ye and your households" (Deut 12:7).

The covenant at Sinai ends with this kind of meal. After the peace offerings, Moses and the elders go up the mountain, "and they saw the God of Israel... also they saw God, and did eat and drink" (Exod 24:5, 9-11). The peace offering is communion: reconciled people at table with God.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/peace-offering
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
If the burnt offering is the gift and the purification offering is the cleansing, the peace offering is the goal: a shared meal in the Father's presence. The whole system aimed at this table.

Paul treats the Lord's Supper the same way: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?... are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?" (1 Cor 10:16-18). Christ "is our peace" (Eph 2:14), and the gospel ends where the prodigal's story ends, with a killed calf and a feast: "let us eat, and be merry: for this my son was dead, and is alive again" (Luke 15:23-24). Salvation is being brought to the table, not just acquitted at the bar.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/peace-offering
blocks.title: Why the penal reading struggles here
blocks.body:
Systematic treatments of atonement in the Reformed tradition built their account mainly on the purification and reparation offerings, read as penal substitution, and gave little weight to the peace offering.

Yet the peace offering does not fit the penal model at all: no one is punished, most of the animal is eaten by the worshippers, and the occasion is often thanksgiving. Recovering it as the goal of the sacrificial system reframes atonement as the restoring of table fellowship between God and his people.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/sin-offering
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Lev 4:1–5:13; 6:24-30).** The offering is graded by the offender's status. For the anointed priest or the whole congregation, a bull's blood is sprinkled seven times before the veil and put on the horns of the incense altar (Lev 4:5-7, 16-18). For a ruler or an ordinary person, the blood is put on the horns of the bronze altar (Lev 4:25, 30). The fat is burned; the meat of the individual's offering is "most holy" and eaten by the priests (Lev 6:25-29).

**Occasions.** It covers sins done "through ignorance" or inadvertently (Lev 4:2), certain failures such as not testifying (Lev 5:1-4), and also states of impurity that involve no wrongdoing: after childbirth (Lev 12:6-8; compare Luke 2:22-24), healing from skin disease (Lev 14:19), and the end of a Nazirite vow (Num 6:14). The poor may bring two birds, and the very poor a little flour (Lev 5:7-13).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/sin-offering
blocks.title: Meaning: purification
blocks.body:
*Chatat* is the same word as "sin", and many Leviticus scholars translate it "purification offering". The reasons are in the text. Its blood is applied **to the sanctuary and altar**, not to the person; it is offered after childbirth, which is not a sin; and on the Day of Atonement it cleanses "the holy place, because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel" (Lev 16:16).

The picture is of God's dwelling among his people being defiled by their sins and impurities, like a home soiled by its occupants. Blood, which is "the life" given by God "upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls" (Lev 17:11), cleanses it so that the Holy One can stay. Leviticus warns that impurity left unaddressed defiles the tabernacle "that is among them" (Lev 15:31).

Deliberate, defiant sin "with a high hand" is not covered by this offering (Num 15:30-31). That points to the need for something more, which Israel met in confession, repentance and the Day of Atonement.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/sin-offering
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
Christ is the purification of God's house. Hebrews says he "by himself purged our sins" (Heb 1:3) and that his blood purges the conscience to serve the living God (Heb 9:14). Like the bull whose body was burned outside the camp, "Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate" (Heb 13:11-12).

Paul uses sin-offering language too. The Greek Old Testament often calls this offering *peri hamartias*, "for sin", and Rom 8:3 says God sent his Son "in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin" (many translations render it "as an offering for sin"), and "condemned sin in the flesh". What is condemned is **sin**, not the Son. The Son enters our defiled humanity and cleanses it from within. As Gregory of Nazianzus put it, what is not assumed is not healed (Letter 101).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/sin-offering
blocks.title: How the penal reading arose
blocks.body:
The traditional English name "sin offering" and the Latin *pro peccato* encouraged a judicial reading: the animal dies the death the sinner deserves. In the Reformed tradition this became the standard account. Calvin presents Christ as bearing in the sinner's place the judgment due to sin (*Institutes* 2.16.5–6), and Charles Hodge treated the Old Testament sacrifices as vicarious punishment, the model for Christ's satisfaction of divine justice.

**Why the relational reading differs.** The text works against a penal account at several points: the offering is required for impurities that carry no guilt (childbirth); a handful of flour can serve for the poor (Lev 5:11-13), and flour cannot die in anyone's place; the meat is "most holy" and eaten by the priests (Lev 6:29), not treated as cursed; and the blood is applied to the sanctuary to cleanse it. The offering deals with defilement that blocks communion, rather than with a debt of punishment.

citations.ref: Systematic Theology, vol. 2, on the satisfaction of Christ

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/sin-offering
blocks.title: Darrin W. Snyder Belousek
blocks.body: Belousek argues that the Levitical sacrifices, including the purification offering, do not operate by penal substitution: the animal's death is not presented as punishment, and atonement is effected through the ritual use of blood, which purifies and restores. He places the cross within a biblical vision of restorative justice rather than retribution.

citations.ref: Atonement, Justice, and Peace (the discussion of sacrifice)

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/guilt-offering
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Lev 5:14–6:7; 7:1-7).** The *asham* covers two kinds of wrong. The first is unintentional misuse of what belongs to God, the "holy things" (Lev 5:15-16). The second is deceiving a neighbour over a deposit, a pledge, a robbery, extortion or lost property and swearing falsely about it (Lev 6:1-5).

In both cases the offender must first **repay in full and add a fifth** (Lev 5:16; 6:5), "in the day of his trespass offering", and only then bring a ram "with thy estimation" in silver shekels (Lev 5:15; 6:6). Num 5:5-8 adds confession and, if the wronged person has died with no kin, payment to the priest. The blood is dashed around the altar and the meat eaten by priests (Lev 7:2-6).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/guilt-offering
blocks.title: Meaning: reparation
blocks.body:
*Asham* means guilt in the sense of liability: the obligation that arises when one has damaged what belongs to another. Many translate it "reparation offering". It is **restorative justice built into worship**: the wronged neighbour is repaid with interest before the offender comes to the altar.

Strikingly, wronging a neighbour is called "a trespass against the LORD" (Lev 6:2). Harm done to a person is harm done to God's household. Isaiah uses this word for the Servant: "when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin (*asham*)... by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many" (Isa 53:10-11).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/guilt-offering
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
The reparation offering shows what reconciliation looks like: repair, restitution and return. Jesus echoes it: "first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift" (Matt 5:23-24). Zacchaeus, met by Jesus' welcome, goes beyond the law's added fifth and restores fourfold (Luke 19:8).

When Isaiah calls the Servant's life an *asham*, the result is that "many" are made righteous (Isa 53:11): relationships restored, a people put right. Christ's self-giving repairs the damage sin has done to God's family and to God's world. It is a gift that makes things whole, not a fine paid to an offended judge.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/guilt-offering
blocks.title: How the penal reading arose
blocks.body:
Isa 53:10 has long been a key text for penal substitution: the Servant is "made an offering for sin" and "it pleased the LORD to bruise him", read as God punishing Christ in our place. Hugo Grotius read Christ's death as a penal example upholding God's moral government (*Defence of the Catholic Faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ*), and Reformed theology after Calvin treated the guilt offering as payment of the penalty due.

**Why the relational reading differs.** In Leviticus the *asham* is not a penalty but **compensation**. The ram follows restitution; it is not the punishment of the offender, and the ram is not punished either. The language belongs to repairing damage to a relationship. Anselm's idea of satisfaction as restoring honour is closer to this than penal theories are, but the Levitical focus is on repairing harm and restoring the wronged party, not on satisfying a requirement for punishment.

citations.ref: A Defence of the Catholic Faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/atonement-goats
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Lev 16).** The high priest takes two goats from the congregation and casts lots: one "for the LORD", one "for Azazel" (Lev 16:7-10). He kills the LORD's goat as a purification offering and sprinkles its blood on and before the mercy seat, as he did with the bull's blood, to cleanse the holy place, the tent and the altar "from the uncleanness of the children of Israel" (Lev 16:15-19).

Then he lays both hands on the head of the live goat, confesses over it "all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins", puts them on its head and sends it away by a man appointed for the purpose: "the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited" (Lev 16:21-22). The Mishnah describes the goat being led out and pushed over a cliff in the wilderness (Mishnah Yoma 6), a later practice not found in Leviticus.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/atonement-goats
blocks.title: Meaning: cleansing and removal
blocks.body:
**Two goats, one act.** The two goats belong together: one cleanses God's dwelling, the other removes the people's sins from the camp altogether. Together they say: the defilement is washed away and the guilt is carried off.

**Who or what is Azazel?** The word appears only in Lev 16 and its meaning is disputed.
- *The goat that departs*: an old reading behind the Latin and the English "scapegoat".
- *A place*: a rugged or remote region.
- *A demonic figure*: the goat is sent to the wilderness power opposed to God. Later Jewish literature names Azazel as a leader of the fallen watchers (1 Enoch 8–10).

In every reading the goat is **not** a sacrifice to Azazel: both goats are presented "before the LORD" (Lev 16:7, 10), and the sending away is God's removal of sin.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/atonement-goats
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
Christ fulfils both goats. As the LORD's goat, he enters the true sanctuary with his own blood and cleanses it, and us (Heb 9:11-14). As the goat that carries sin away, he is "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29): "as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us" (Ps 103:12).

On a Christus Victor reading, sin is sent back to the realm of chaos and death where it belongs, and the powers that held God's people are stripped of their claim. The goal of the day is the same as the goal of the gospel: God living with a cleansed people, and his people free to draw near.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/atonement-goats
blocks.title: How the penal reading arose
blocks.body:
Popular penal accounts fuse the two goats into one picture: sins are laid on the victim, and the victim is killed under God's wrath in the sinner's place. This fusion became common in Protestant preaching and is assumed in many systematic treatments of the atonement that follow Calvin and Hodge.

**Why the relational reading differs.** In Lev 16 the two actions are distinct. The goat that is killed has no sins placed on it; its blood is used to **cleanse** the sanctuary. The goat that bears the sins is **not killed**; it carries them away alive. Leviticus never presents the slain goat as absorbing wrath. Reading the day as punishment combines what the text keeps apart.

citations.ref: Systematic Theology, vol. 2, on the satisfaction of Christ

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/atonement-goats
blocks.title: Michael S. Heiser on Azazel
blocks.body: Heiser reads Azazel as a wilderness demonic figure. He stresses that the goat is not an offering to Azazel: rather, Israel's sins are sent away from sacred space to the realm outside God's order, where they belong.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/red-heifer
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Num 19).** A red heifer without blemish that has never borne a yoke is killed outside the camp in the presence of Eleazar the priest, who sprinkles its blood toward the front of the tent seven times. It is burned whole, skin, flesh, blood and dung, with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet thrown into the fire (Num 19:2-6). A clean man gathers the ashes and keeps them outside the camp.

Anyone who touches a corpse is unclean for seven days and must be sprinkled with the ash-water on the third and seventh days (Num 19:11-12, 17-19). Oddly, those who prepare and sprinkle it become unclean themselves until evening (Num 19:7-10, 21). The Mishnah tractate Parah describes the rite and lists the few heifers prepared in Israel's history (Mishnah Parah 3).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/red-heifer
blocks.title: Meaning: purification from death
blocks.body:
Num 19:9 calls the ash-water "a purification for sin" (*chatat*): it is a kind of purification offering. Its target is the most powerful impurity in the Torah, contact with the dead.

In Israel's worldview death is the opposite of the living God, and its contagion has to be kept away from his dwelling (Num 19:13, 20). The heifer, the red colour, the cedar and scarlet all point to life and blood; the "running" water is literally "living water" (Num 19:17). The rite does not deal with moral guilt at all. Burying your dead was a duty, not a sin, but it still required cleansing before approaching God.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/red-heifer
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
Hebrews makes the comparison: "if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh: how much more shall the blood of Christ... purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?" (Heb 9:13-14).

In the Gospels the contagion runs the other way. Jesus touches the bier of the widow's son and takes the dead girl by the hand (Luke 7:14; 8:54). Instead of death defiling him, his life overcomes death. He is the living water that cleanses from death itself.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/red-heifer
blocks.title: Why the penal reading struggles here
blocks.body: Because it is called a purification offering, the red heifer is sometimes folded into a general penal account of sacrifice. But there is no sin here to be punished, no transfer of guilt and no wrath; corpse contact is a state, not a crime. The rite is about cleansing from death so that God's people can approach him, which is how Hebrews uses it.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/passover-lamb
blocks.title: How it was offered
blocks.body:
**Procedure (Exod 12).** A lamb per household (shared with neighbours if the household is small) is chosen on the 10th and killed at twilight on the 14th (Exod 12:3-6). Its blood is struck on the lintel and doorposts with a bunch of hyssop (Exod 12:7, 22). The meat is roasted, not boiled, eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs by people ready to travel, and no bone is broken (Exod 12:8-11, 46). No uncircumcised person may eat it, but a circumcised foreigner may (Exod 12:48).

**Later practice.** Deuteronomy moves the killing to the central sanctuary (Deut 16:2, 5-7). In the Second Temple period the lambs were slaughtered in the temple court and eaten in Jerusalem (Mishnah Pesachim 5). See also the Passover festival entry.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/passover-lamb
blocks.title: Meaning: belonging and liberation
blocks.body:
Exodus does not describe the Passover lamb as a sin offering, and nothing is confessed over it. Its blood is "a token" (sign) on the houses (Exod 12:13); the destroyer passes over the homes so marked (Exod 12:23). The night is about God's judgment on Pharaoh and "all the gods of Egypt" (Exod 12:12) and the release of his firstborn son, Israel (Exod 4:22-23).

The lamb is also food. The whole household eats it together, so the sacrifice ends in a family meal. Later, the firstborn of Israel are consecrated to God in memory of this night (Exod 13:2, 11-15).

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/passover-lamb
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body:
John the Baptist calls Jesus "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29). John's Gospel notes that no bone of his was broken (John 19:36), Paul calls him "our passover" (1 Cor 5:7), and Peter says we were redeemed, that is, set free from slavery, "with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish" (1 Pet 1:18-19).

The Passover lamb is the clearest Old Testament picture of **Christus Victor**. God defeats the power that holds his children, marks them as his own, and brings them out to a meal and a journey home. In Revelation the slain Lamb stands on the throne and has "prevailed" (Rev 5:5-6). His blood does not buy off the Father; it is the Father's own act of rescue through the Son.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/passover-lamb
blocks.title: How the penal reading arose
blocks.body:
Popular preaching often reads the Passover as the clearest case of penal substitution: God's wrath would have struck Israel's firstborn, but it fell on the lamb instead. This merges Passover with a later, penal reading of the sin offering, a merger common in Protestant teaching shaped by Calvin's account of Christ bearing the penalty due to sinners (*Institutes* 2.16.5–6).

**Why the relational reading differs.** Exodus does not say the lamb was punished or that it bore anyone's sin. The blood is a **sign** of the households under God's protection, and the story's enemy is Pharaoh, not the Father. The lamb is then eaten in a family meal. Reading it as a penal transaction imports a framework the text does not supply.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/passover-lamb
blocks.title: Justin Martyr
blocks.body: Justin argues that the Passover lamb was a type of Christ, and observes that the lamb was roasted on spits arranged in the form of a cross.

blocks.subject: entry:sacrifice/passover-lamb
blocks.title: Melito of Sardis
blocks.body: Melito's homily retells the Passover night and declares that the lamb's slaying, the blood and the exodus found their meaning in Christ, the Lamb who was led to the slaughter and rose to set his people free.
