blocks.subject: entry:law/categories-of-the-law
blocks.title: Where the division came from
blocks.body:
The Torah presents its commands as one covenant teaching, often mixing what later readers would separate. Lev 19 puts "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (19:18) next to rules about mixed seed and fabrics (19:19). Rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments (Babylonian Talmud, Makkot 23b) without dividing them into moral and ritual classes.

**How the division developed:**
- In the second century the Valentinian teacher Ptolemy, in his *Letter to Flora*, sorted the law into a pure part (the Decalogue) that the Saviour fulfilled, a part mixed with injustice (such as "eye for eye") that he abolished, and a symbolic part (sacrifices, circumcision, Sabbath) that he transformed into spiritual realities.
- Augustine distinguished precepts for living a good life from precepts that symbolised what was to come (*Contra Faustum* 6.2).
- Thomas Aquinas gave the classic form: the Old Law contains **moral**, **ceremonial** and **judicial** precepts; the moral endure, the ceremonial are fulfilled in Christ, and the judicial lapsed with Israel's polity (*Summa Theologiae* I-II q.99 a.4; qq.103–104).
- Calvin adopted the threefold scheme (*Institutes* 4.20.14–16), and the Westminster Confession made it confessional: ceremonial laws are abrogated and judicial laws "expired together with the State of that people" (Westminster Confession 19.3–4).

blocks.subject: entry:law/categories-of-the-law
blocks.title: Strengths and weaknesses of the scheme
blocks.body:
**Strengths.** The division explains why Christians do not offer sacrifices or keep food laws but still treat "thou shalt not steal" as binding. It reflects real differences the New Testament itself recognises (Mark 7:19; Heb 9–10).

**Weaknesses.** The New Testament usually treats the law as a single whole: whoever keeps it must keep all of it (Gal 5:3; Jas 2:10). Some commands sit awkwardly in the scheme; the Sabbath is in the Ten Commandments yet is also a sign and a ceremonial day (Col 2:16-17). Critics argue that the scheme can let readers decide in advance what still applies, instead of asking how each law is fulfilled in Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:law/categories-of-the-law
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus did not come "to destroy the law, or the prophets... but to fulfil" (Matt 5:17). He is the lens for all of it. Some laws are fulfilled by being completed (the sacrifices in his self-offering), some by being deepened to the heart (anger and lust, Matt 5:21-30), and some by being opened up to all nations (food laws, Mark 7:19; Acts 10).

The thread through every command is love. "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets" (Matt 22:40), and "love is the fulfilling of the law" (Rom 13:10). Because Jesus is the clearest picture of the Father, each law is best read by asking what love it was protecting and how Jesus embodied it, rather than by sorting it into a box first.

blocks.subject: entry:law/ten-commandments
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Scripture calls them "the ten words" (Exod 34:28; Deut 4:13; 10:4). They begin not with a command but with a relationship: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage" (Exod 20:2). The commands describe how a freed people lives with the God who freed them and with each other.

They appear twice, with small differences: the Sabbath is grounded in creation in Exod 20:11 and in the exodus in Deut 5:15. Traditions number them differently: Jewish tradition counts Exod 20:2 as the first word; Catholics and Lutherans join the commands about other gods and images and split the command on coveting; Orthodox and Reformed churches count the command against images separately. Many scholars compare their shape with ancient Near Eastern treaties, in which a great king recounts what he has done before stating obligations.

blocks.subject: entry:law/ten-commandments
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus reads the commandments from the inside. Murder begins in contempt, adultery in the look of the heart (Matt 5:21-30). When the rich man asks what to do, Jesus lists the second table and then invites him to follow (Mark 10:17-22): the commandments lead to a person.

Paul sums up the second table in one word: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Rom 13:9). The new covenant promise is that God writes this law on hearts (Jer 31:33). For the children of God the Ten Words are less a bar of judgment than a description of the family likeness: what life looks like when it shares the Father's love.

blocks.subject: entry:law/shema
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
"Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might" (Deut 6:4-5). *Shema* means "hear", with the sense of heeding and obeying. The confession is followed by teaching: these words are to be on the heart, taught to children, spoken at home and on the road, bound on hand and forehead, and written on doorposts (Deut 6:6-9).

In Jewish practice the Shema (Deut 6:4-9; 11:13-21; Num 15:37-41) is recited morning and evening. The Mishnah opens with the rules for its recitation and describes saying it as taking on "the yoke of the kingdom of heaven" (Mishnah Berakhot 1–2; 2:2). The tassels, phylacteries (*tefillin*) and doorpost scroll (*mezuzah*) come from these passages.

blocks.subject: entry:law/shema
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus began with the Shema itself, "Hear, O Israel", and joined it to love of neighbour (Mark 12:29-31). Love for God is the response to being loved first: the God who says "our God" has already claimed Israel as his own, and "we love him, because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19).

Paul restates the Shema with Jesus inside it: "to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things... and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things" (1 Cor 8:6). The oneness of God is not solitude. It is the shared life of the Father, the Son and the Spirit, and the Shema's call to love with the whole self is an invitation into that communion.

blocks.subject: entry:law/love-your-neighbour
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Lev 19 opens, "Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2), and then defines holiness in everyday terms: leave the edges of the field for the poor, pay wages the same day, do not curse the deaf or trip the blind, judge fairly, do not slander, do not hate your brother in your heart. The chapter's climax is "thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD" (19:18).

In context "neighbour" first means a fellow Israelite. But the same chapter extends the command: the stranger who lives among you "shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself" (19:34). The Talmud preserves Hillel's summary of the Torah to a would-be convert: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; the rest is commentary (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a).

blocks.subject: entry:law/love-your-neighbour
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus joins Lev 19:18 to the Shema (Matt 22:37-40). When a lawyer asks, "who is my neighbour?", Jesus tells of a Samaritan who stops for a wounded man and turns the question around: which one "was neighbour" to him? (Luke 10:29-37). Then he widens love to enemies, "that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven" (Matt 5:44-45).

Finally he gives a new measure: "love one another; as I have loved you" (John 13:34). Love of neighbour is what holiness looks like when it is the Father's own holiness. It is a family likeness, not an external rule, and Paul can say that the whole law is fulfilled in this one word (Gal 5:14).

blocks.subject: entry:law/love-the-stranger
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
The *ger* is a resident foreigner without land or kin in Israel. The Torah repeatedly forbids oppressing him, grounding the command in memory: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Exod 23:9). He shares in the Sabbath rest (Exod 20:10), the festivals (Deut 16:11, 14), the gleanings (Lev 19:10) and the triennial tithe (Deut 14:28-29), and the same law applies to him as to the native-born (Lev 24:22).

The command reaches its height in Deuteronomy: God "doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment. Love ye therefore the stranger" (Deut 10:18-19).

blocks.subject: entry:law/love-the-stranger
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Israel is to love the stranger because God does. In Jesus the Father himself comes as a stranger: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in" (Matt 25:35). The hero of Jesus' parable of neighbour-love is a Samaritan, an outsider (Luke 10:33).

In Christ the outsiders are brought into the household: "ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (Eph 2:19). The law of the stranger was a sketch of the Father's adoption of the nations.

blocks.subject: entry:law/sabbath-commandment
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
The commandment forbids ordinary work on the seventh day for everyone in the household, including servants, animals and foreigners (Exod 20:8-11). Other laws forbid kindling fire (Exod 35:3) and gathering sticks (Num 15:32-36), and the prophets condemn carrying loads through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath (Jer 17:21-27). It is "a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever" (Exod 31:17).

Later Jewish law worked out what counts as work in great detail (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists thirty-nine categories). Christians have long disagreed about the Sabbath: some (for example the Westminster Confession, 21.7–8) treat the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath under a moral command; others see the Sabbath as fulfilled in Christ and the Lord's Day as a new feast of resurrection.

blocks.subject: entry:law/sabbath-commandment
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Most of Jesus' conflicts with the religious leaders happen on the Sabbath, and almost all of them involve healing. He argues that the Sabbath is for doing good and saving life (Mark 3:4), that animals are watered and rescued on it, so a daughter of Abraham should be freed on it (Luke 13:15-16), and that his work continues the Father's own work: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (John 5:17).

The Sabbath was always about freedom: rest for slaves, release for the bound. Jesus, "Lord also of the sabbath" (Mark 2:28), brings it to its goal, the rest of being at home with the Father (Matt 11:28-30; Heb 4:9-10).

blocks.subject: entry:law/purity-laws
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Leviticus distinguishes **holy and common, clean and unclean** (Lev 10:10). Impurity comes mainly from three sources: death (touching a corpse, Num 19), the loss of life-fluids such as blood and semen (Lev 12; 15), and the skin disease often translated "leprosy" (*tsara'at*, Lev 13–14). It spreads by contact, lasts for set periods, and is removed by waiting, washing and sometimes offerings.

Impurity is **not** the same as sin. Giving birth, burying a parent or having a normal period made a person unclean without any wrongdoing. The concern is God's presence: "Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness; that they die not in their uncleanness, when they defile my tabernacle that is among them" (Lev 15:31). The common thread is that the God of life is kept apart from what speaks of death.

blocks.subject: entry:law/purity-laws
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
In the Gospels contagion runs the other way. Jesus touches a man with skin disease, and instead of becoming unclean, he makes him clean (Mark 1:41). A woman with a twelve-year flow of blood touches him and is healed, and power goes out from him (Mark 5:29-30). He takes a dead girl by the hand and raises her (Mark 5:41).

Holiness in Jesus is not fragile; it overflows. He declares that what defiles is what comes out of the heart (Mark 7:15, 20-23), and the early church learns not to call any person common or unclean (Acts 10:28). The purity laws pictured a God of life who could not live with death; in Christ that God enters our death and fills it with life.

blocks.subject: entry:law/food-laws
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves may be eaten; sea creatures need fins and scales; certain birds and most insects are forbidden (Lev 11; Deut 14). Blood may never be eaten (Lev 17:10-14), and a kid is not to be boiled in its mother's milk (Deut 14:21).

The Torah gives its own reason: the food laws mirror Israel's separation from the nations. "I am the LORD your God, which have separated you from other people. Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean" (Lev 20:24-25). In the Second Temple period they became a badge of faithfulness, as with Daniel (Dan 1:8) and the Maccabean martyrs who died rather than eat pork (2 Macc 6–7). Ancient and modern writers have proposed hygienic, symbolic and anthropological explanations; none commands agreement.

blocks.subject: entry:law/food-laws
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus taught that nothing entering a person from outside can defile, and Mark adds, "purging all meats", that is, making all foods clean (Mark 7:18-19). Peter's vision of the sheet (Acts 10) is first about food, but Peter draws the real lesson: "God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean" (Acts 10:28).

The food laws marked a boundary between Israel and the nations. When the Father opens his family to the nations in Christ, the boundary marker is no longer needed, and the shared table becomes the sign of the new family (Gal 2:11-14; Rom 14:14-17).

blocks.subject: entry:law/jubilee
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
After seven sabbaths of years, the trumpet sounds on the Day of Atonement of the forty-ninth year to begin the fiftieth: "proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you" (Lev 25:9-10). Land returns to the families who first received it, and Israelites who sold themselves as servants go free (Lev 25:10, 13, 39-41).

The reason is theological: "the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me" (Lev 25:23). Land prices were calculated by the years remaining to the jubilee (Lev 25:15-16). The word *deror*, "liberty", reappears in Isa 61:1 and Jer 34:8. How often, or whether, the jubilee was actually kept is debated; there is little direct historical evidence. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the text known as 11QMelchizedek links the jubilee and Isa 61 with a heavenly deliverer figure called Melchizedek.

blocks.subject: entry:law/jubilee
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus read Isa 61, "to preach deliverance to the captives... to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord", and said, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears" (Luke 4:18-21). The Greek word for "deliverance" and "liberty" there, *aphesis*, is the word the Greek Old Testament used for the jubilee release in Lev 25, and it is the same word Luke uses for "forgiveness" (Luke 24:47).

Forgiveness in Jesus is jubilee: debts cancelled, captives freed, the lost inheritance restored. Salvation is not only a verdict but a homecoming, children restored to their Father's land as heirs (Rom 8:17).

blocks.subject: entry:law/sabbatical-year
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
In the seventh year the land rests, and whatever grows of itself is for the poor and the animals (Exod 23:10-11; Lev 25:1-7). Every seventh year is also "the LORD's release": creditors cancel debts owed by fellow Israelites (Deut 15:1-3), and Hebrew servants go free with generous provision (Deut 15:12-15).

Deuteronomy anticipates the objection that no one will lend as the release approaches and forbids hard-hearted calculation (Deut 15:9-10). "There shall be no poor among you" is the goal (Deut 15:4), even though "the poor shall never cease out of the land" (Deut 15:11). Chronicles links the exile to the neglected sabbatical years (2 Chr 36:21; Lev 26:34-35). The Mishnah records Hillel's *prosbul*, a legal device that let loans survive the seventh year so that lending would not dry up (Mishnah Sheviit 10:3-4).

blocks.subject: entry:law/sabbatical-year
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus taught his disciples to pray, "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Matt 6:12), and told of a servant forgiven an unpayable debt who would not release a small one (Matt 18:23-35). The sabbatical release becomes the shape of life in the kingdom.

The first church in Jerusalem lived it out: "neither was there any among them that lacked" (Acts 4:34), echoing Deut 15:4. A Father who forgives freely forms children who release one another.

blocks.subject: entry:law/gleaning
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
"When ye reap the harvest of your land, thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest... thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger" (Lev 19:9-10). Forgotten sheaves and the last of the olives and grapes are also left "for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow" (Deut 24:19-21). A hungry traveller may pick grain by hand from a neighbour's field, though not with a sickle (Deut 23:25).

The poor are not handed charity; they harvest for themselves, with dignity. The Mishnah tractate Peah opens by listing things that have no fixed measure, among them the corner of the field and acts of loving-kindness (Mishnah Peah 1:1). In Ruth, Boaz goes beyond the law and tells his workers to drop extra grain for her (Ruth 2:15-16).

blocks.subject: entry:law/gleaning
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus' disciples pluck grain as they walk through a field on the Sabbath (Mark 2:23), using exactly the right Deut 23:25 grants. The dispute is about the Sabbath, not theft.

Gleaning builds generosity into the structure of the economy. In Ruth, the gleaner from Moab becomes part of the family through a kinsman-redeemer, and an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Ruth 4:13-17; Matt 1:5). The Father's provision for the outsider ends in adoption.

blocks.subject: entry:law/cities-of-refuge
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Ancient Israel had no police force; a dead man's nearest kinsman, the "avenger of blood" (*go'el haddam*), pursued the killer. The Torah limits this by setting apart six cities, three on each side of the Jordan: Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron; Bezer, Ramoth and Golan (Josh 20:7-8). The roads to them were to be prepared (Deut 19:3).

The congregation judges between murder and accidental killing (Num 35:16-25). The deliberate murderer is handed over; the accidental killer lives in the city "unto the death of the high priest", and then may go home (Num 35:25, 28). The Mishnah tractate Makkot discusses the law of exile to these cities and records that the high priest's mother provided food and clothing for the exiles so they would not pray for her son's death (Mishnah Makkot 2:6).

blocks.subject: entry:law/cities-of-refuge
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus never mentions the cities of refuge, so this is a reading through the lens of Hebrews, which speaks of us "who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us", an anchor that enters behind the veil "whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever" (Heb 6:18-20).

The law protected the person who had done harm without intent and set them free by the death of the high priest. In Christ, the High Priest has died and lives for ever, so the release is complete. On the cross he prayed for those who did not know what they were doing (Luke 23:34). The Father's justice makes room for refuge and return, not only for retribution.

blocks.subject: entry:law/eye-for-an-eye
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
The formula "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" appears three times (Exod 21:24; Lev 24:20; Deut 19:21), each in a court setting. It limits punishment to what fits the harm, against the escalating revenge of Lamech's "seventy and sevenfold" (Gen 4:23-24). It also applies equally: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for one of your own country" (Lev 24:22). The Code of Hammurabi has similar rules, but graded by social class.

Even within the Torah the formula often meant compensation: a master who knocks out a servant's eye or tooth must set the servant free (Exod 21:26-27). The Mishnah takes injury law as monetary, listing payments for damage, pain, healing, loss of time and shame (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1).

blocks.subject: entry:law/eye-for-an-eye
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus quotes the formula and then goes further: "resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also" (Matt 5:38-39). In an honour-and-shame culture a blow to the right cheek was most likely a back-handed insult; turning the other cheek refuses both retaliation and humiliation. Then he grounds it in the Father: love your enemies "that ye may be the children of your Father", who sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matt 5:44-45).

This matters for how we picture God's justice. If Jesus, the perfect picture of the Father, sets aside retaliation, then the cross is not the place where God finally gets his eye for an eye. It is where God absorbs evil and overcomes it with good (Rom 12:17-21). God's justice is restorative: it sets things right.

blocks.subject: entry:law/kinsman-redeemer
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
The *go'el* is the next of kin who acts for a family member in trouble. He buys back land a poor relative had to sell (Lev 25:25), redeems a relative who sold himself to a foreigner (Lev 25:47-49), and, in another role, avenges a murdered relative (Num 35:19). The related duty of levirate marriage, raising up a son for a brother who died childless (Deut 25:5-10), is combined with redemption of land in Ruth 4.

God takes this family title for himself: "I will redeem you with a stretched out arm" (Exod 6:6); "Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine" (Isa 43:1). Job hopes, "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25).

blocks.subject: entry:law/kinsman-redeemer
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Redemption in the Bible is a family act. Only a relative could redeem, so the Son becomes our relative: "both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren... as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same" (Heb 2:11, 14).

Jesus says he came "to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). The ransom is not paid to the Father, as if the Father held the family hostage. The kinsman pays what it costs to bring his people home, and the aim is restoration: land returned, family line restored, the outsider Ruth brought into the house.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/creation-covenant
blocks.title: A disputed covenant
blocks.body:
**The case for.** Gen 1–2 has many features of a covenant: God creates a relationship, gives a vocation (Gen 1:28), sets a boundary with a warning (Gen 2:16-17) and offers life (the tree of life, Gen 2:9; 3:22). Hos 6:7 can be read "they like Adam have transgressed the covenant". Jeremiah speaks of God's "covenant of the day" and "of the night" (Jer 33:20, 25), suggesting a covenant with creation itself. Irenaeus counted four covenants, the first "under Adam" (*Against Heresies* 3.11.8).

**The case against.** The word *berit* does not appear in Gen 1–3; its first use is with Noah (Gen 6:18). Hos 6:7 may mean "like men" or refer to the town of Adam (Josh 3:16: "the city Adam"). Many scholars therefore speak of a creation *relationship* rather than a formal covenant.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/creation-covenant
blocks.title: How the 'covenant of works' reading arose
blocks.body:
In sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Reformed "federal" theology this relationship became the **covenant of works**: God promised Adam life on condition of perfect obedience, with death as the penalty (Westminster Confession 7.2). Christ was then seen as fulfilling the terms Adam broke and bearing the penalty, a framework developed systematically by later Reformed theologians such as Charles Hodge.

**How the relational reading differs.** Genesis presents Adam first as a son and image-bearer living in God's gift, not as a worker earning a wage. Luke's genealogy ends "Adam, which was the son of God" (Luke 3:38). The command in Gen 2 protects a relationship of trust; it is not a contract for earning life. Sin is the breaking of communion, and its fruit is death because cutting oneself off from the source of life is death.

citations.ref: Systematic Theology, vol. 2, on the covenant of works

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/creation-covenant
blocks.title: Christ, the last Adam
blocks.body: Paul calls Adam "the figure of him that was to come" (Rom 5:14). Where Adam grasped and fell, the last Adam receives everything as Son and gives himself away (1 Cor 15:45; Phil 2:6-8). Christ does not merely fix a broken contract; he restores the image and the sonship Adam lost, and brings humanity into the communion it was made for.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/creation-covenant
blocks.title: Irenaeus: recapitulation
blocks.body: Irenaeus teaches that when the Son became incarnate he 'recapitulated' (summed up) in himself the long history of humanity, so that what we lost in Adam, being in the image and likeness of God, we might recover in Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/noahic-covenant
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
This is the first use of the word "covenant" in the Bible (Gen 6:18). After the flood God promises, without conditions, "neither shall all flesh be cut off any more by the waters of a flood" (Gen 9:11). The covenant includes "every living creature", not only humans (Gen 9:10, 12, 15).

The sign is God's "bow" (*qeshet*), the ordinary word for a war bow. Many interpreters see the image of a warrior hanging up his weapon. Gen 9 also restates the creation blessing ("be fruitful, and multiply", 9:1), allows meat but forbids eating blood, and protects human life because humans are made in God's image (9:3-6). Rabbinic tradition later derived seven "Noahide" commandments binding on all humanity (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 56a); some scholars compare these with the requirements for Gentile believers in Acts 15:20, 29.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/noahic-covenant
blocks.title: Christ and the covenant with Noah
blocks.body:
God's covenant with Noah is a promise to the whole world, and its fulfilment is cosmic. Isaiah links it to "the covenant of my peace" that shall not be removed (Isa 54:9-10). Peter sees the flood as a picture of baptism, saving "by the resurrection of Jesus Christ" (1 Pet 3:20-21).

In Christ, God reconciles "all things unto himself... having made peace through the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20). The bow hung in the cloud becomes a cross raised on a hill: God's final answer to the world's violence is not another flood but his Son.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/abrahamic-covenant
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
The promise comes first (Gen 12:1-3) and is then sealed as a covenant. In Gen 15 Abram believes God, "and he counted it to him for righteousness" (15:6). Then God tells him to cut animals in two. A smoking furnace and a burning lamp, signs of God's presence, pass between the pieces while Abram sleeps (15:17). In the ancient world those who walked between cut animals invoked the animals' fate on themselves if they broke faith (compare Jer 34:18-20). Here **only God** walks the path.

In Gen 17 God renames Abram and Sarai, gives circumcision as the sign, and states the heart of every covenant: "to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee" (Gen 17:7). After the binding of Isaac, God confirms the promise with an oath (Gen 22:16-18).

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/abrahamic-covenant
blocks.title: Christ and the covenant with Abraham
blocks.body:
Paul says the Scripture "preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed" (Gal 3:8). The promised seed is ultimately Christ (Gal 3:16), and all who belong to Christ, Jew and Gentile, "are Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise" (Gal 3:29). The promise even grows: Abraham is "heir of the world" (Rom 4:13).

This is a family promise. God binds himself to a man and his children and opens that family to the nations. Its fulfilment is a growing kingdom: blessing spreading through all the families of the earth until "the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea" (Hab 2:14).

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/mosaic-covenant
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
The order matters. Rescue comes before law: "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself" (Exod 19:4). Only then: "if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me" (19:5).

The covenant is sealed when Moses sprinkles "the blood of the covenant" on the altar and the people (Exod 24:6-8) and the elders eat and drink in God's presence (24:9-11). Its blessings and curses are set out in Lev 26 and Deut 28. Deuteronomy already looks beyond Israel's failure to a day when "the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart" (Deut 30:6). Scholars often compare the covenant's structure with ancient treaties between a great king and his vassal.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/mosaic-covenant
blocks.title: Christ and the covenant at Sinai
blocks.body:
At the Last Supper Jesus echoes Exod 24:8: "this is my blood of the new testament [covenant]" (Matt 26:28). Paul calls the law a *paidagogos*, a household guardian over a child "until the time appointed of the father", so that "we might receive the adoption of sons" (Gal 3:24; 4:1-5). Sinai was a stage in the upbringing of God's son Israel, not the final form of the family.

Hebrews says the first covenant "is ready to vanish away" (Heb 8:13). Written before the temple fell in AD 70, the phrase fits a partial-preterist reading in which the old covenant order passed away with the temple, while its purpose, a people who know God, is fulfilled in Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/mosaic-covenant
blocks.title: James B. Torrance: covenant, not contract
blocks.body: James Torrance distinguishes a **covenant** from a **contract**. A contract is conditional: blessing is earned by meeting terms. A covenant is a promise of grace that calls for a response but does not depend on it. He argues that the indicatives of grace come before the imperatives of law, as at Sinai where 'I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out' comes before the commandments.

citations.ref: Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/priestly-covenant
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Several texts speak of a covenant with the priests. The priests' share of the holy offerings is "a covenant of salt for ever" (Num 18:19), salt standing for permanence. After Phinehas turns back God's anger in the plague of Baal-Peor, God gives him "my covenant of peace... the covenant of an everlasting priesthood" (Num 25:12-13).

Malachi recalls "my covenant... with Levi" as "life and peace": the priest was to teach truth and turn many from iniquity, "for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts" (Mal 2:4-7). Jeremiah sets the Levitical covenant alongside the Davidic one as sure as day and night (Jer 33:17-22), and Nehemiah complains of priests who had "defiled... the covenant of the priesthood" (Neh 13:29).

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/priestly-covenant
blocks.title: Christ the faithful priest
blocks.body:
Hebrews argues that the priesthood has changed: Jesus is a priest "after the order of Melchisedec", not by descent from Levi but "after the power of an endless life" (Heb 7:11-16). He fulfils the priestly covenant's promise of a lasting priesthood by being the priest who never dies (Heb 7:24-25).

He also shares it. His people become "a royal priesthood" (1 Pet 2:9) and "kings and priests unto God and his Father" (Rev 1:6). Christ is the true worshipper who brings us with him into the Father's presence.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/priestly-covenant
blocks.title: James B. Torrance: the priesthood of Christ
blocks.body: James Torrance stresses the priesthood of Christ: Jesus, as our High Priest, offers the true worship of humanity to the Father, and Christian worship is the gift of participating through the Spirit in the Son's communion with the Father, rather than something we do to win God's favour.

citations.ref: Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/davidic-covenant
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
David wants to build God a house; God answers that he will build David a house, a dynasty (2 Sam 7:5, 11). The promise centres on David's son: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Sam 7:14). If he sins he will be disciplined, "but my mercy shall not depart away from him" (7:15). "Thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever" (7:16).

The text does not call it a covenant, but later Scripture does (Ps 89:3, 28; 2 Sam 23:5). Ps 2 has God tell the king, "Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee" (Ps 2:7). Ps 89 wrestles with the promise when the dynasty falls, and the prophets keep it alive (Isa 9:6-7; 55:3; Jer 23:5).

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/davidic-covenant
blocks.title: Christ the Son of David
blocks.body:
Gabriel tells Mary that God will give her son "the throne of his father David... and of his kingdom there shall be no end" (Luke 1:32-33). Paul says Jesus was "declared to be the Son of God with power... by the resurrection from the dead" (Rom 1:3-4), and Hebrews applies 2 Sam 7:14 to him (Heb 1:5).

At its heart the Davidic covenant is about sonship: the king is God's son. Peter proclaims that God raised Jesus to sit on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36). He is reigning now, and "he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet" (1 Cor 15:25). The kingdom has begun and is growing until it fills the earth.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/new-covenant
blocks.title: Biblical basis
blocks.body:
Jeremiah, writing as the old covenant order collapsed, promised "a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers... I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people... for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest" (Jer 31:31-34).

Ezekiel adds cleansing water, a new heart and God's own Spirit within (Ezek 36:25-27), and calls it "a covenant of peace... an everlasting covenant" with God's dwelling among them (Ezek 37:26-27). The Dead Sea Scrolls community also spoke of itself as entering a "new covenant", which shows that the hope was alive in Jesus' day.

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/new-covenant
blocks.title: Christ the mediator of the new covenant
blocks.body:
"This cup is the new testament [covenant] in my blood, which is shed for you" (Luke 22:20). Jesus inaugurates the new covenant with his own life, and Paul calls himself a minister "of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit" (2 Cor 3:6). Hebrews quotes Jeremiah at length to show that Christ is its mediator (Heb 8:6-13; 10:15-18).

Its centre is knowing God: "they shall all know me". Jesus defines eternal life the same way: "that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent" (John 17:3). The new covenant is not a better contract but a restored family, children who know their Father from the inside because the Spirit of the Son lives in them (Gal 4:6).

blocks.subject: entry:covenant/new-covenant
blocks.title: Irenaeus: the four covenants
blocks.body: Irenaeus speaks of four principal covenants given to the human race: under Adam, under Noah, the giving of the law under Moses, and the fourth, which renews humanity and sums up all things in itself through the gospel.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/gate
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The courtyard was 100 by 50 cubits, enclosed by white linen hangings five cubits high (Exod 27:9-18). There was only one entrance, on the east side, a twenty-cubit screen woven in blue, purple and scarlet (Exod 27:13-16). Anyone approaching God came from the east and moved westward, toward the presence.

The gate was wide, unlike the narrow doors of the inner tent. In Eden the way back was guarded on the east by cherubim (Gen 3:24); in the tabernacle, God provides a way in from the east.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/gate
blocks.title: Christ the door
blocks.body:
"I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture" (John 10:9). "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6).

The single gate is not a restriction but an invitation. The Father has made a way back to himself, and the way is a person, his Son, who opens his house to all who come.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/bronze-altar
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The altar of burnt offering stood in the courtyard between the gate and the tent (Exod 40:6, 29). It was a hollow frame of acacia wood covered in bronze, with horns at its four corners, carried on poles (Exod 27:1-8). All the animal and grain offerings were burned on it, and the blood of most offerings was dashed against it or put on its horns.

Its fire first came "out from before the LORD" (Lev 9:24) and was to be kept burning continually (Lev 6:13). The horns of the altar were a place of refuge (1 Kgs 1:50).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/bronze-altar
blocks.title: Christ and the altar
blocks.body:
"We have an altar" (Heb 13:10), says Hebrews, meaning the cross where Jesus "suffered without the gate" (13:12). The first thing a worshipper met inside the gate was the place of offering; the first thing we meet in the gospel is the self-giving of the Son.

The altar fire was God's presence receiving the gift. At the cross the Son offers himself to the Father in love "through the eternal Spirit" (Heb 9:14), and the Father receives the offering as "a sweetsmelling savour" (Eph 5:2).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/laver
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The laver stood between the altar and the tent. Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet there before entering the tent or serving at the altar, "that they die not" (Exod 30:18-21). No size or shape is given.

It was made from the bronze mirrors of "the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle" (Exod 38:8). Solomon's temple later had a great bronze "sea" and ten smaller basins (1 Kgs 7:23-39).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/laver
blocks.title: Christ and the washing
blocks.body:
On the night before he died Jesus took a basin and washed his disciples' feet. "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" (John 13:8). The Lord of the tabernacle does the priest's washing himself, for his friends.

The New Testament speaks of "the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost" (Titus 3:5) and of drawing near "having our bodies washed with pure water" (Heb 10:22). Those cleansed by the Son are brought in as priests who can serve in the Father's house.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/holy-place
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The tent was made of upright acacia boards overlaid with gold, covered by four layers: inner curtains of fine linen in blue, purple and scarlet with cherubim, then goats' hair, rams' skins dyed red, and an outer covering of fine leather (Exod 26:1-30). The boards give an interior of about 30 by 10 cubits, divided by the veil into the holy place (about 20 cubits long) and the most holy place.

In the holy place were the lampstand on the south, the table on the north and the incense altar before the veil (Exod 26:35; 40:22-27). The priests went in daily (Heb 9:6). Josephus interpreted the tabernacle's three parts as an image of the cosmos, sea and land open to all and heaven reserved for God (*Antiquities* 3.7.7).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/holy-place
blocks.title: Christ and the holy place
blocks.body:
Inside the holy place everything spoke of a household: light, bread on a table, and fragrance. It was the room where the priests lived out their service in God's house.

In Christ the whole people are priests (1 Pet 2:5, 9) and the church itself is the dwelling: "ye are the temple of God, and... the Spirit of God dwelleth in you" (1 Cor 3:16). Christians do not visit the holy place; they live in it, as sons and daughters at home in the Father's house (John 14:2, 23).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/lampstand
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The lampstand stood on the south side of the holy place, opposite the table (Exod 26:35). It was beaten out of a single talent of pure gold, with a central stem and three branches on each side, decorated with cups "made like unto almonds", knobs and flowers (Exod 25:31-39). Its seven lamps burned pure olive oil "from the evening unto the morning before the LORD" (Exod 27:20-21; Lev 24:2-4).

Its almond-tree design has suggested to many readers a stylised tree of life. Zechariah saw a lampstand fed by two olive trees: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD" (Zech 4:6).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/lampstand
blocks.title: Christ the light
blocks.body:
At the Feast of Tabernacles, when great lamps lit the temple court, Jesus said, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life" (John 8:12).

He also says, "Ye are the light of the world" (Matt 5:14). In Revelation the risen Christ walks among seven golden lampstands, which are the churches (Rev 1:12-13, 20). The light of the Son, fed by the oil of the Spirit, shines through his people into the world.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/table-of-showbread
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The table stood on the north side of the holy place (Exod 26:35). On it were twelve loaves in two rows, with frankincense, renewed every Sabbath "on behalf of the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant"; the old loaves were eaten by the priests in the holy place (Lev 24:5-9).

The Hebrew name is *lechem panim*, literally "bread of the face" or "bread of the presence" (Exod 25:30). Twelve loaves for twelve tribes, set before God's face, picture Israel's life held continually in his presence, and the table recalls the covenant meal at Sinai where the elders "saw God, and did eat and drink" (Exod 24:11). When David and his men were hungry, the priest gave them this holy bread (1 Sam 21:6).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/table-of-showbread
blocks.title: Christ the bread
blocks.body:
Jesus cited David eating the bread of the presence to show that mercy comes before ritual (Matt 12:3-7). And he called himself "the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger" (John 6:35).

The table in God's house was set for the twelve tribes; Jesus sets a table for the twelve and, through them, for the world (Luke 22:14-20, 29-30). The bread of the presence becomes the bread of communion, the Father feeding his family at his own table.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/altar-of-incense
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The incense altar stood "before the vail that is by the ark of the testimony" (Exod 30:6). The priest burned a special blend of incense on it every morning and evening when he tended the lamps (Exod 30:7-8, 34-38). Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, its horns were cleansed with blood (Exod 30:10).

Zechariah was serving at this altar when Gabriel appeared to him (Luke 1:8-11). Hebrews lists a golden *thumiaterion* among the furnishings of the most holy place (Heb 9:4); interpreters debate whether this means the incense altar (closely tied to the inner room) or a censer.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/altar-of-incense
blocks.title: Christ the intercessor
blocks.body:
"Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense" (Ps 141:2). In Revelation the incense rises "with the prayers of all saints" before God's throne (Rev 8:3-4).

Christ "ever liveth to make intercession" for us (Heb 7:25). Our prayers rise to the Father not on their own merit but joined to the Son's prayer, in the Spirit who intercedes within us (Rom 8:26, 34). Prayer is a share in the conversation of the Trinity.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/veil
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The veil (*parokhet*) divided "the holy place and the most holy" (Exod 26:33). Woven into it were cherubim (Exod 26:31), the guardians who had barred the way back to Eden (Gen 3:24). Only the high priest went past it, once a year, and not without blood (Lev 16:2; Heb 9:7).

Herod's temple had its own great curtain. Josephus describes it as a Babylonian tapestry of blue, scarlet, linen and purple, depicting the heavens (*Jewish War* 5.5.4).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/veil
blocks.title: Christ the way through
blocks.body:
When Jesus died, "the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom" (Matt 27:51). The tear went from top to bottom: God himself opened the way.

Hebrews says we enter "by a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh" (Heb 10:20). The way into the Father's presence is through the humanity of the Son. The cherubim no longer bar the way; we come in, in him, "with a true heart in full assurance of faith" (Heb 10:22).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/most-holy-place
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
Behind the veil was the most holy place (literally "holy of holies"), containing only the ark of the covenant (Exod 26:33-34). Its dimensions in the tabernacle are inferred from the boards as a cube of about ten cubits; in Solomon's temple the inner sanctuary was a cube of twenty cubits overlaid with gold (1 Kgs 6:20).

It was the throne room of the invisible King. No light from outside, no furniture but the ark, and entry only for the high priest on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:2, 34; Heb 9:7).

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/most-holy-place
blocks.title: Christ and the holy of holies
blocks.body:
In Revelation the New Jerusalem is a cube, its length, breadth and height equal (Rev 21:16), and there is no temple in it, "for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it" (21:22). The whole city has become the most holy place: "the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them" (21:3).

Through Christ the place once entered by one man once a year is open to all God's children: "having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus" (Heb 10:19). The Father's goal was never a locked room but a shared home.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/ark-and-mercy-seat
blocks.title: Description
blocks.body:
The ark held the two tablets of the testimony (Exod 25:16), and Hebrews adds the jar of manna and Aaron's rod that budded (Heb 9:4; Exod 16:33; Num 17:10). Over it was the *kapporet*, a slab of pure gold with two cherubim facing each other, wings spread over it (Exod 25:17-20).

The point of it all is relationship: "there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims" (Exod 25:22; Num 7:89). God is "the LORD of hosts, which dwelleth between the cherubims" (1 Sam 4:4), and the ark is his footstool (1 Chr 28:2). On the Day of Atonement blood was sprinkled on and before the *kapporet* (Lev 16:14-15).

*Kapporet* is related to *kipper*, "to make atonement". The Greek Old Testament rendered it *hilasterion*; William Tyndale gave English the phrase "mercy seat".

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/ark-and-mercy-seat
blocks.title: Christ the mercy seat
blocks.body:
Paul says God set forth Christ as a *hilasterion* (Rom 3:25), the same word used for the mercy seat. Christ is the place where God and humanity meet, where the blood that cleanses is applied, and where God's presence and his people are reconciled.

Read this way, the mercy seat is not a place where wrath is bought off, but the throne of grace where God says, "there I will meet with thee". Hebrews invites us: "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy" (Heb 4:16). In Jesus the meeting place has a human face.

blocks.subject: entry:tabernacle/ark-and-mercy-seat
blocks.title: How the penal reading arose
blocks.body:
The King James Version translates *hilasterion* in Rom 3:25 as "propitiation", a word meaning the appeasing of an angry party. Through the Latin *propitiatio* and the Reformation emphasis on God's justice satisfied, Rom 3:25 became a central proof text for penal substitution: Christ's death turns aside God's wrath against sinners (Calvin, *Institutes* 2.16.2–6; Hodge's *Systematic Theology*).

**How the relational reading differs.** In the Greek Old Testament *hilasterion* is chiefly the name of the **mercy seat** itself (Exod 25:17-22; compare Heb 9:5), the place where blood cleanses and God meets his people. In Rom 3:25 it is God who sets Christ forth; God is the subject of the reconciling act, not its object. Reading it as "mercy seat" or "place of atonement" keeps Paul's image tied to the meeting place of Exod 25.

citations.ref: Systematic Theology, vol. 2, on the satisfaction of Christ

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-hagar
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
Hagar, pregnant and fleeing Sarai's harsh treatment, is found by "the angel of the LORD" at a spring in the wilderness (Gen 16:7). The angel speaks in God's own voice: "I will multiply thy seed exceedingly" (16:10), a promise only God can make.

The narrator then says "she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me" (*El Roi*, 16:13). The first person in Scripture to give God a name is a foreign slave woman, and she does so because God came looking for her.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-hagar
blocks.title: Who is the angel of the LORD?
blocks.body:
Who is "the angel of the LORD"? Three main answers have been given.

- **The pre-incarnate Son.** From Justin Martyr onward many Christian writers held that the one who appears and speaks as God is the Word, who always makes the invisible Father known (John 1:18).
- **A created angel speaking for God.** Augustine argued that we cannot tell which person of the Trinity appeared, and that the appearances were brought about through angels (*On the Trinity*, books 2–3). On this view the angel speaks in God's name the way an ambassador speaks for a king.
- **A visible form of God himself.** Many modern scholars, without deciding the Trinitarian question, note that the text identifies the angel with the LORD while also distinguishing him from the LORD.

The text itself holds the tension: the angel is sent by the LORD, yet speaks as the LORD.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-hagar
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body: Whatever one's view of the angel's identity, the God revealed here is the one Jesus shows: he seeks the outcast, hears the afflicted (the name Ishmael means "God hears", 16:11) and gives a future to someone the family had cast off.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/visitors-at-mamre
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
"And the LORD appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre" (Gen 18:1). Abraham sees three men, runs to welcome them and serves them a meal (18:2-8). One of them promises a son to Sarah and is called "the LORD" (18:10, 13-14). As two go on toward Sodom, "Abraham stood yet before the LORD" and intercedes for the city (18:22-33). The two who arrive in Sodom are called angels (19:1).

God comes to Abraham as a guest, eats at his table and talks with him as a friend (compare Isa 41:8; Jas 2:23).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/visitors-at-mamre
blocks.title: One, or three?
blocks.body:
- Justin Martyr argued that the one called "the LORD" among the three was the Word, "another God" distinct from the Father in number though not in will, and that the other two were angels (*Dialogue with Trypho* 56).
- A later tradition, famous through Andrei Rublev's fifteenth-century icon, sees the three visitors as a figure of the Trinity.
- Many interpreters read the scene as a theophany of the LORD accompanied by two angels, without identifying a particular person of the Trinity.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/visitors-at-mamre
blocks.title: Justin Martyr
blocks.body: Justin uses the Mamre story to argue with Trypho that the one who appeared to Abraham and was called God and Lord is distinct from the Father who made all things, and is the one Christians know as Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-at-moriah
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
As Abraham raises the knife, "the angel of the LORD called unto him out of heaven" and stops him: "now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me" (Gen 22:11-12). Note "from **me**". The angel speaks as the one to whom Isaac was being offered.

He calls a second time: "By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD" (22:16), and repeats the promise of blessing for all nations (22:18). Abraham names the place "The LORD will provide" (*YHWH yireh*, 22:14).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-at-moriah
blocks.title: Who is the angel of the LORD?
blocks.body:
Who is "the angel of the LORD"? Three main answers have been given.

- **The pre-incarnate Son.** From Justin Martyr onward many Christian writers held that the one who appears and speaks as God is the Word, who always makes the invisible Father known (John 1:18).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-at-moriah
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body: The angel's intervention is the turning point of the story: God does not want Isaac's death. The God who appears at Moriah stops a sacrifice and provides one himself. That is the logic of the gospel: the Father does not demand a son from us; he gives his own (Rom 8:32).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/jacobs-wrestler
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
"And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day" (Gen 32:24). The man cannot overcome Jacob but dislocates his hip with a touch, refuses to give his name, and renames him Israel, "for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men" (32:28). Jacob names the place Peniel: "for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved" (32:30).

Hosea recalls it: "he had power with God: yea, he had power over the angel" (Hos 12:3-4). Near death, Jacob blesses Joseph's sons in the name of "God, before whom my fathers... did walk, the God which fed me... The Angel which redeemed me from all evil" (Gen 48:15-16), setting God and the Angel in parallel.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/jacobs-wrestler
blocks.title: Man, angel or God?
blocks.body: The wrestler is called a man (Gen 32:24), God (32:28, 30) and an angel (Hos 12:4). Readers have taken him as the pre-incarnate Son (Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho* 58), as an angel representing God, or as a visible manifestation of God whom the narrator deliberately leaves mysterious. Some modern critics see an older story of a river spirit behind the account, though in Genesis as it stands Jacob meets the God of his fathers.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/jacobs-wrestler
blocks.title: Michael S. Heiser
blocks.body: Heiser points to Gen 48:15-16, where the God of Abraham and Isaac and 'the Angel' who redeemed Jacob are fused into a single blessing, as evidence that the Angel was understood to be God himself in visible form, one of the passages he uses to describe a 'second Yahweh' figure in the Old Testament.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/burning-bush
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
"And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush" (Exod 3:2). When Moses turns aside, "God called unto him out of the midst of the bush" (3:4): "I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham" (3:6). He reveals his name, "I AM THAT I AM" (3:14), and his purpose: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people... and I am come down to deliver them" (3:7-8).

Stephen retells the scene with the same overlap: the angel appeared in the flame, and "the voice of the Lord came unto him" (Acts 7:30-31).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/burning-bush
blocks.title: Who is the angel of the LORD?
blocks.body:
Who is "the angel of the LORD"? Three main answers have been given.
