blocks.subject: entry:christophany/burning-bush
blocks.title: Justin Martyr
blocks.body: Justin argues that the one who spoke to Moses from the bush, called both angel and God, cannot be the Father who never leaves the heavens, but is the one who ministers the Father's will: the Son.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/burning-bush
blocks.title: Irenaeus
blocks.body: Irenaeus teaches that it was the Son of God who spoke with Moses at the bush, coming down to save his people, and that the Old Testament appearances of God were the Word rehearsing the incarnation.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-with-the-name
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
"Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way... Beware of him, and obey his voice, provoke him not; for he will not pardon your transgressions: for my name is in him" (Exod 23:20-21). In the Old Testament God's *name* stands for his own presence (Deut 12:5; 1 Kgs 8:29).

The angel of God moved with the pillar of cloud at the Red Sea (Exod 14:19). Isaiah, looking back, says "the angel of his presence saved them: in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; and he bare them, and carried them" (Isa 63:9).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-with-the-name
blocks.title: Michael S. Heiser: "my name is in him"
blocks.body: Heiser treats Exod 23:20-23 as a key text: because God's Name, that is his very presence, is 'in' the Angel, the Angel is Yahweh in a second, visible form, distinct from yet identified with the Yahweh who sends him. Heiser describes this as a 'two Yahwehs' pattern that later Jewish and Christian thought had to reckon with.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-with-the-name
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body: Jesus speaks of the Father's name in a similar way: "I have manifested thy name" and "keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me" (John 17:6, 11). The God who carried Israel in love through the wilderness is the God whose name Jesus reveals as Father.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/commander-of-the-army
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body: Near Jericho Joshua sees "a man over against him with his sword drawn". To the question, "Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?" he answers, "Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come" (Josh 5:13-14). Joshua falls down and worships, and is told, "Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy" (5:15), the same words spoken to Moses at the bush (Exod 3:5). The next verse continues, "And the LORD said unto Joshua" (6:2).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/commander-of-the-army
blocks.title: Michael or the LORD?
blocks.body:
- **A christophany.** The commander accepts worship and makes the ground holy, as at the bush; Justin Martyr counted this among the appearances of the Son (*Dialogue with Trypho* 62).
- **The archangel Michael.** Others identify him with Michael, the "prince" who fights for Israel (Dan 10:13, 21; 12:1), noting that he is not explicitly called God.
- The flow from Josh 5:15 to 6:2 ("And the LORD said") suggests to many readers that the commander and the LORD are the same speaker, though the chapter break may be artificial.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/commander-of-the-army
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body: His answer, "Nay", refuses to be recruited to anyone's side. God is not a tribal deity; Joshua must ask whether he is on God's side. The same Lord later commands his followers to put the sword away (Matt 26:52) and wins his victory at the cross.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-gideon
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
"And there came an angel of the LORD, and sat under an oak" (Judg 6:11). He greets Gideon, "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour" (6:12), and in the next breath "the LORD looked upon him, and said, Go in this thy might" (6:14). The narrator moves freely between "the angel of the LORD" and "the LORD".

The angel touches Gideon's offering with his staff, fire consumes it, and he vanishes. Gideon cries, "Alas, O Lord GOD! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face", and the LORD says, "Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die" (6:21-23). Earlier the angel of the LORD had spoken at Bochim in God's first person: "I made you to go up out of Egypt" (Judg 2:1).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-gideon
blocks.title: Who is the angel of the LORD?
blocks.body:
Who is "the angel of the LORD"? Three main answers have been given.

- **The pre-incarnate Son.** From Justin Martyr onward many Christian writers held that the one who appears and speaks as God is the Word, who always makes the invisible Father known (John 1:18).
- **A created angel speaking for God.** Augustine argued that we cannot tell which person of the Trinity appeared, and that the appearances were brought about through angels (*On the Trinity*, books 2–3). On this view the angel speaks in God's name the way an ambassador speaks for a king.
- **A visible form of God himself.** Many modern scholars, without deciding the Trinitarian question, note that the text identifies the angel with the LORD while also distinguishing him from the LORD.

The text itself holds the tension: the angel is sent by the LORD, yet speaks as the LORD.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-gideon
blocks.title: Michael S. Heiser
blocks.body: Heiser cites the Gideon story as an example of the angel and Yahweh being presented as two persons in one scene who are nonetheless both identified as Yahweh, part of his case for a visible 'second Yahweh' in the Hebrew Bible.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-manoah
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
The angel of the LORD appears to Manoah's wife and then to Manoah, announcing a son who will be a Nazirite (Judg 13:3-14). His appearance is "like the countenance of an angel of God, very terrible" (13:6). When Manoah asks his name, he answers, "Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?" (13:18), using a Hebrew word (*peli*) related to *pele*, "Wonderful", in Isa 9:6.

As the offering burns, "the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame of the altar" (13:20). Manoah concludes, "We shall surely die, because we have seen God" (13:22).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-manoah
blocks.title: Who is the angel of the LORD?
blocks.body:
Who is "the angel of the LORD"? Three main answers have been given.

- **The pre-incarnate Son.** From Justin Martyr onward many Christian writers held that the one who appears and speaks as God is the Word, who always makes the invisible Father known (John 1:18).
- **A created angel speaking for God.** Augustine argued that we cannot tell which person of the Trinity appeared, and that the appearances were brought about through angels (*On the Trinity*, books 2–3). On this view the angel speaks in God's name the way an ambassador speaks for a king.
- **A visible form of God himself.** Many modern scholars, without deciding the Trinitarian question, note that the text identifies the angel with the LORD while also distinguishing him from the LORD.

The text itself holds the tension: the angel is sent by the LORD, yet speaks as the LORD.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/angel-and-manoah
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body: Manoah's wife reasons better than her husband: if the LORD wanted to kill us, he would not have received our offering or told us these things (Judg 13:23). The God who appears is gracious, and his name is "Wonderful", a title Isaiah gives the child who will be born (Isa 9:6).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/word-of-the-lord
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
"After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram in a vision, saying, Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield" (Gen 15:1). The word then "brought him forth abroad" to look at the stars (15:5). A word that leads someone outside is behaving like a person.

At Shiloh, "the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel" (1 Sam 3:10), and "the LORD revealed himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the LORD" (3:21). When "the word of the LORD came" to Jeremiah, "the LORD put forth his hand, and touched my mouth" (Jer 1:4, 9). Later Aramaic translations (Targums) often speak of God's *Memra*, his "Word", as the agent of his presence and action.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/word-of-the-lord
blocks.title: Idiom or person?
blocks.body: Most interpreters read "the word of the LORD came" as an idiom for prophetic revelation, not a visible person. Others argue that in texts like Gen 15 and 1 Sam 3 the Word is presented as standing, leading and touching, and so anticipates John's "the Word was made flesh" (John 1:14). The Targums' use of *Memra* is debated too: some see a near-personal figure, others a reverent way of avoiding direct statements about God.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/word-of-the-lord
blocks.title: Michael S. Heiser: the Word as a person
blocks.body: Heiser argues that in passages such as Gen 15:1-5 and 1 Sam 3, 'the word of the LORD' is presented as a visible, embodied figure who comes, stands and leads, and that John's prologue draws on this Old Testament picture of the Word as Yahweh made visible.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/word-of-the-lord
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... And the Word was made flesh" (John 1:1, 14). The God who spoke to Abram and stood by the boy Samuel has always been the God who speaks to be known. In Jesus the Word is no longer heard in a vision; he eats with sinners and calls God "Father".

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/fourth-man-in-the-fire
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
Nebuchadnezzar looks into the furnace and says, "Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God" (Dan 3:25, KJV). Afterward he blesses God, "who hath sent his angel, and delivered his servants" (3:28).

Isaiah had promised: "when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned... For I am the LORD thy God" (Isa 43:2-3).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/fourth-man-in-the-fire
blocks.title: Angel or the Son?
blocks.body:
The Aramaic phrase *bar elahin* can mean "a son of the gods", that is, a divine being, which is how most modern translations render it; the KJV's "the Son of God" reflects the Christian reading. The speaker is a pagan king, and he himself calls the figure God's "angel" (Dan 3:28).

- Many Christian readers, from the early church onward, have seen here the pre-incarnate Son present with his people in suffering.
- Others read the figure as an angel sent by God, which is how the king describes it.

Either way, the point of the story is that God is with his faithful servants in the fire.

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/fourth-man-in-the-fire
blocks.title: A relational reading
blocks.body: God does not keep his servants out of the furnace; he comes into it with them. That is the shape of the incarnation: the Son enters our fire, our suffering and our death, and walks us out unharmed. "Lo, I am with you alway" (Matt 28:20).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/melchizedek
blocks.title: The text
blocks.body:
After Abram rescues Lot, "Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God" (Gen 14:18). He blesses Abram, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything (14:19-20). He appears without introduction and disappears without comment.

Ps 110:4 addresses the king-messiah: "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek". Hebrews develops this: Melchizedek is "without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God" (Heb 7:3). Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, 11QMelchizedek presents Melchizedek as an exalted heavenly figure who brings jubilee release, and the Talmud records a rabbinic tradition that identified him with Shem (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 32b).

blocks.subject: entry:christophany/melchizedek
blocks.title: Christophany or type?
blocks.body:
- **A type, not an appearance (majority view).** Melchizedek was a real Canaanite priest-king. Hebrews' "without father, without mother" argues from the silence of Genesis: his genealogy is not recorded, so he stands as a picture of an eternal priesthood. "Made like unto the Son of God" (Heb 7:3) implies likeness, not identity.
- **A christophany (minority view).** Some interpreters take Heb 7:3 literally and see Melchizedek as the pre-incarnate Son himself.
- **A heavenly figure.** 11QMelchizedek shows that some Jews in the Second Temple period saw Melchizedek as an angelic or heavenly deliverer.

blocks.subject: entry:number/one
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body:
"The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deut 6:4). The same word, *echad*, describes husband and wife becoming "one flesh" (Gen 2:24), the people answering "with one voice" (Exod 24:3), and the two sticks that become "one" in Ezekiel's hand (Ezek 37:17).

In the New Testament Jesus says, "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30), and prays that his followers "may be one, as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee" (John 17:21). Paul lists "one body, and one Spirit... one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all" (Eph 4:4-6).

blocks.subject: entry:number/one
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: The meaning of "one" comes from context, not from the number itself. It is fair to say that biblical oneness is often relational: God's oneness is a shared life, and he makes his people one by drawing them into it (John 17:21). It is not fair to treat *echad* as a secret code for the Trinity. The doctrine of the Trinity rests on how the New Testament speaks of the Father, the Son and the Spirit, not on the grammar of one Hebrew word.

blocks.subject: entry:number/three
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body:
"The third day" is a recurring moment of meeting or rescue: Abraham sees Moriah on the third day (Gen 22:4); God comes down on Sinai on the third day (Exod 19:11, 16); Hosea says "in the third day he will raise us up" (Hos 6:2); Jonah is in the fish "three days and three nights" (Jon 1:17). Paul says Christ "rose again the third day according to the scriptures" (1 Cor 15:4).

Threefold repetition also marks emphasis: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts" (Isa 6:3), Peter's three denials and Jesus' three questions, "lovest thou me?" (John 21:15-17).

blocks.subject: entry:number/three
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Three is a natural number for emphasis and for stories (beginning, middle, end). The "third day" pattern is meaningful because the New Testament itself points to it (1 Cor 15:4; Matt 12:40). Elsewhere, enjoy the echoes but hold them lightly. Counting threes in a passage and calling each one Trinitarian turns reading into puzzle-solving.

blocks.subject: entry:number/four
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body: Four rivers flow out of Eden to water the earth (Gen 2:10-14). God gathers his scattered people "from the four corners of the earth" (Isa 11:12) and breathes life "from the four winds" (Ezek 37:9). Ezekiel sees four living creatures with four faces (Ezek 1:5-10), and Revelation sets four living creatures around the throne (Rev 4:6-8). Daniel's visions have four kingdoms rising from the sea stirred by "the four winds of the heaven" (Dan 7:2-3).

blocks.subject: entry:number/four
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Irenaeus argued that there must be exactly four Gospels because there are four zones of the world and four principal winds (*Against Heresies* 3.11.8). The conclusion was right, but the argument shows the risk: the number did not make the Gospels four; the churches' reception of them did. Four in Scripture usually signals completeness of extent, "the whole world", and should be read that way rather than mined for hidden meanings.

blocks.subject: entry:number/four
blocks.title: Irenaeus on the four Gospels
blocks.body: Irenaeus argues that the Gospels could be neither more nor fewer than four, because there are four zones of the world and four principal winds, and the church is spread throughout the world; he compares the four Gospels to the four faces of the cherubim.

blocks.subject: entry:number/six
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body: God makes humankind on the sixth day (Gen 1:26-31), and "six days shalt thou labour" (Exod 20:9). Some boastful figures are marked by six: Goliath is six cubits and a span tall, with a spearhead of six hundred shekels of iron (1 Sam 17:4-7); Nebuchadnezzar's golden image is sixty cubits high and six wide (Dan 3:1). Solomon's yearly gold income is 666 talents (1 Kgs 10:14). Revelation calls 666 "the number of a man" (Rev 13:18).

blocks.subject: entry:number/six
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Six is first of all the number of ordinary work and of humanity as created, and that is good (Gen 1:31). Associations with arrogance (Goliath, Nebuchadnezzar) are suggestive, but the Bible never says "six is the number of imperfection". Use the word "suggestive" rather than "means" when making such connections.

blocks.subject: entry:number/seven
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body:
God finishes creation and rests on the seventh day (Gen 2:2-3). The pattern repeats in the Sabbath, the seventh year of release (Deut 15:1), the jubilee after seven sevens of years (Lev 25:8), the seven days of Unleavened Bread and Tabernacles, and sevenfold sprinklings of blood (Lev 4:6; 16:14). Jericho is circled seven times on the seventh day (Josh 6:15).

In Hebrew the word for seven (*sheva*) sounds like the verb "to swear an oath" (*shava*), and Abraham's oath at Beersheba ("well of the oath" or "well of seven") involves seven lambs (Gen 21:28-31). Revelation is built on sevens: churches, seals, trumpets, bowls. Jesus' "seventy times seven" (Matt 18:22) turns the number of completeness into limitless forgiveness.

blocks.subject: entry:number/seven
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Seven is the clearest case of symbolic number in the Bible, because the text itself builds on it. Even so, the symbolism serves the story: creation's rest, covenant faithfulness, complete forgiveness. Hunting for sevens in word counts or letter patterns ("Bible codes") is not how the biblical writers signal meaning and tends to lead readers away from what the passage actually says.

blocks.subject: entry:number/ten
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body: The covenant at Sinai is summed up in "ten words" (Exod 34:28). Egypt suffers ten plagues (Exod 7–12). The tithe is a tenth (Lev 27:30). Jacob complains that Laban changed his wages "ten times" (Gen 31:7). Daniel asks for a test of ten days (Dan 1:12), Jesus tells of ten virgins (Matt 25:1), and the church at Smyrna is told it will have tribulation "ten days" (Rev 2:10). In later Jewish practice ten men form the quorum for communal prayer.

blocks.subject: entry:number/ten
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Many uses of ten are simply round numbers, like "ten times" in English. The ten words are meaningful because they form a complete, memorable summary that can be counted on two hands. Read "ten days" in Revelation as a limited, short period rather than an exact count.

blocks.subject: entry:number/twelve
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body:
Jacob's twelve sons become the twelve tribes (Gen 49:28). Moses sets up twelve pillars at Sinai (Exod 24:4); the high priest wears twelve stones (Exod 28:21); twelve loaves sit on the table of presence (Lev 24:5). Elijah builds an altar of twelve stones (1 Kgs 18:31).

Jesus chooses twelve apostles (Matt 10:1-4) and promises they will sit on twelve thrones "judging the twelve tribes of Israel" (Matt 19:28). After the feeding of the five thousand twelve baskets are left over (Mark 6:43). The New Jerusalem has twelve gates named for the tribes and twelve foundations named for the apostles (Rev 21:12-14).

blocks.subject: entry:number/twelve
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Jesus' choice of twelve was a deliberate sign that he was reconstituting Israel around himself, a point widely recognised by scholars. Twelve therefore means the people of God, gathered and complete. It is not a key for chronology, and multiples of twelve should be read as multiplying that meaning, not as numbers to calculate with.

blocks.subject: entry:number/forty
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body: Rain falls forty days and nights in the flood (Gen 7:12). Moses is on the mountain forty days and nights (Exod 24:18), and Israel wanders forty years, a year for each day of spying (Num 14:33-34). Elijah walks forty days to Horeb (1 Kgs 19:8). Nineveh is given forty days (Jon 3:4). Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness (Matt 4:2) and appears to the disciples for forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1:3). Several judges and kings rule forty years (Judg 3:11; 2 Sam 5:4).

blocks.subject: entry:number/forty
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: The repeated forty creates a pattern: Jesus' forty days in the wilderness deliberately echo Israel's forty years, and where Israel failed, the beloved Son trusts his Father. Partial-preterist readers also note that about forty years, a biblical generation, passed between Jesus' words in Matt 24:34 and the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. That is a reasonable observation, but using forty to calculate future dates has a long record of failure.

blocks.subject: entry:number/seventy
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body:
The table of nations in Gen 10 lists about seventy peoples, and Jacob's family going down to Egypt numbers seventy (Exod 1:5). Moses appoints seventy elders to share the Spirit (Num 11:16-17, 25). Jeremiah prophesies seventy years of exile (Jer 25:11), and Daniel receives a vision of "seventy weeks" (seventy sevens) until the anointed one and the end of sin (Dan 9:24-27). Jesus sends out seventy (some manuscripts read seventy-two) messengers (Luke 10:1). Seventy bulls were offered at Tabernacles (Num 29:12-34), which the Talmud links with the nations of the world.

Deut 32:8 says God divided the nations "according to the number of the children of Israel" in the traditional Hebrew text; the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek Old Testament read "the sons of God".

blocks.subject: entry:number/seventy
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Seventy's link with the nations makes Jesus' sending of the seventy suggestive: a mission that anticipates the gospel going to every people. Daniel's seventy weeks are best read in connection with the first coming of Christ and the events of the first century (Dan 9:24-27), as many partial-preterist and historic interpreters hold, rather than as a timetable with a postponed final week. Seventy itself is a full, round number and should be handled that way.

blocks.subject: entry:number/seventy
blocks.title: Michael S. Heiser on Deuteronomy 32:8
blocks.body: Heiser argues that the reading 'sons of God' in Deut 32:8 is original, and that it reflects a worldview in which the nations (numbered at seventy in Gen 10) were placed under lesser divine beings after Babel, while Israel was kept as the LORD's own portion. In his reading, the gospel reclaiming the nations is the undoing of that division.

blocks.subject: entry:number/144000
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body:
John "heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel" (Rev 7:4), twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes (7:5-8). The list is irregular: Dan is missing, Levi is included, and Joseph appears alongside his son Manasseh. Then John looks and sees "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations" (7:9). In Rev 14:1-5 the 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion.

The number is 12 × 12 × 1,000: the people of God, squared and multiplied.

blocks.subject: entry:number/144000
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Revelation often pairs what John hears with what he sees: he hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb (Rev 5:5-6); he hears 144,000 from Israel and sees a countless multitude from all nations (7:4, 9). Many interpreters therefore take the two as the same people described two ways. Partial-preterist readers take the sealed as the Jewish believers protected through the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. In any case, the number is a symbol of a complete, ordered people of God, not a cap on how many are saved. Groups that treat it as a literal elite (for example, Jehovah's Witnesses) build a great deal on a symbol.

blocks.subject: entry:number/666
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body:
Revelation invites the reader to "count" the number, "for it is the number of a man" (Rev 13:18). In Hebrew and Greek, letters double as numbers, so names have numerical values (gematria).

The most widely held identification is **Nero Caesar**. Written in Hebrew letters as *Nron Qsr*, the name adds up to 666. Some early manuscripts read **616**, which matches the Latin spelling *Nero Caesar* without the final *n*. Irenaeus knew of the 616 reading (*Against Heresies* 5.30.1).

blocks.subject: entry:number/666
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Irenaeus himself warned against confident guessing. He listed possible names but said it was safer to wait for the fulfilment than to speculate (*Against Heresies* 5.30.3). A partial-preterist reading fits the text's own clues: John's readers could calculate it, and Rev 17:10 places the beast within their era. The Nero link, together with the 616 variant, makes that reading strong. What should be avoided is the endless search for a new antichrist in each generation, which has produced fear and failed predictions rather than understanding.

blocks.subject: entry:number/666
blocks.title: Irenaeus on the number
blocks.body: Irenaeus knew manuscripts reading 616 and judged 666 the correct reading, found in the oldest copies. He suggested possible names (such as Euanthas, Lateinos and Teitan) but counselled that it was safer to await the fulfilment of the prophecy than to guess at the name.

blocks.subject: entry:number/1000
blocks.title: Where the number appears
blocks.body: God keeps covenant "to a thousand generations" (Deut 7:9; compare Ps 105:8). "Every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills" (Ps 50:10). "A thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday" (Ps 90:4; 2 Pet 3:8). In Rev 20:1-7 Satan is bound for a thousand years, and the martyrs live and reign with Christ for a thousand years.

blocks.subject: entry:number/1000
blocks.title: Reading it wisely
blocks.body: Augustine read the thousand years as either the final period of history or, more likely, a number of perfection standing for the whole time of the church, during which Christ reigns and the devil is bound (*City of God* 20.7). Postmillennial interpreters likewise take it as the long, indefinite age in which Christ reigns from heaven and the gospel gradually fills the earth. Premillennialists take it as a future literal reign after Christ's return. Given how the Bible uses "thousand" elsewhere, building precise timetables on the number is unwise; its point is the long and complete triumph of Christ's reign.

blocks.subject: entry:number/1000
blocks.title: Augustine on the thousand years
blocks.body: Augustine offers two readings of the thousand years: either the last thousand years of world history, or, as he prefers, a number of perfection (ten cubed) standing for the whole period of the church's history, during which the devil is bound and the saints reign with Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:number/1000
blocks.title: B. B. Warfield
blocks.body: Warfield read Rev 20:1-10 as a picture of the security of the saints who have died and now reign with Christ in heaven during the present age, rather than as a future earthly reign; the 'thousand years' is a symbol of completeness, not a literal period.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/adam-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body:
Adam is made in God's image to rule creation (Gen 1:26-28) and is formed from dust and filled with God's breath (Gen 2:7). Luke's genealogy calls him "the son of God" (Luke 3:38). Through his disobedience death enters the world (Gen 3; Rom 5:12).

Paul uses the Greek word *typos*: Adam "is the figure (*typos*) of him that was to come" (Rom 5:14). The contrast runs through Rom 5:12-21 and 1 Cor 15: "as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Cor 15:22); "the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit" (1 Cor 15:45).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/adam-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Christ is not simply a better individual; he is a new head for humanity. What Adam lost, Christ restores and surpasses: sonship, the image of God, communion and dominion. Where Adam grasped at being like God, the Son "thought it not robbery to be equal with God" yet emptied himself (Phil 2:6-7).

This is the heart of **recapitulation**: the Son goes back over the human story, obeying where Adam disobeyed, at a tree where Adam fell at a tree, and so brings humanity home to the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/adam-and-christ
blocks.title: Irenaeus: obedience at the tree
blocks.body: Irenaeus teaches that the disobedience committed at a tree was undone by the Son's obedience on the tree, so that in the second Adam we are reconciled to God, having been made his enemies in the first.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/adam-and-christ
blocks.title: Athanasius: the Word renews the image
blocks.body: Athanasius explains that the Word took a human body so that, by offering it to death on behalf of all, he might undo the corruption that had come upon humanity, and renew in us the image in which we were made.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/adam-and-christ
blocks.title: James M. Hamilton Jr.
blocks.body: Hamilton treats Adam as a foundational type: later figures such as Noah, Abraham, Israel and David are presented in Adamic terms, and the pattern escalates until it is fulfilled in Christ, the last Adam.

citations.ref: Typology: Understanding the Bible's Promise-Shaped Patterns

blocks.subject: entry:typology/isaac-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: God tells Abraham, "Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest" (Gen 22:2). Isaac carries the wood up the mountain (22:6); father and son go "both of them together" (22:6, 8); Abraham says, "God will provide himself a lamb" (22:8). On the third day (22:4) Abraham receives his son back, which Hebrews calls receiving him "in a figure" (Heb 11:19). Chronicles places Solomon's temple on "mount Moriah" (2 Chr 3:1).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/isaac-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
The language returns at Jesus' baptism: "Thou art my beloved Son" (Mark 1:11), and in Paul: God "spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all" (Rom 8:32). Like Isaac, Jesus carries the wood (John 19:17).

The difference matters as much as the likeness. At Moriah God stops the sacrifice: he does not want Isaac's death, and he provides the ram himself. At the cross the Father does not demand a son from us; he gives his own, and the Son gives himself. Father and Son go "both of them together".

blocks.subject: entry:typology/joseph-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body:
Joseph is his father's favourite son (Gen 37:3), hated by his brothers, sold for silver (37:28) and presumed dead. He suffers unjustly, then is raised to the right hand of Pharaoh, and all the world comes to him for bread (41:39-57). His brothers come to him, and he forgives them: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass... to save much people alive" (50:20).

The New Testament never calls Joseph a type in so many words, but Stephen tells his story in a way that prepares for Jesus: "the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt: but God was with him" (Acts 7:9).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/joseph-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
The pattern of the rejected one who becomes the saviour of those who rejected him runs straight to Jesus: "him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken... whom God hath raised up" (Acts 2:23-24).

Joseph's tears and embrace (Gen 45:14-15) show what the exalted Christ does with the brothers who betrayed him. He does not take revenge. He reveals himself, forgives, and brings the whole family to live with him, as the Father's purpose was all along.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/moses-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: Moses is rescued as a baby from a king's massacre (Exod 1:22–2:10), leads God's people out of slavery, meets God on the mountain, gives the law, and intercedes for the people, even offering to be blotted out for them (Exod 32:32). God spoke with him "mouth to mouth" (Num 12:8). He promised: "The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee... like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken" (Deut 18:15).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/moses-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Matthew tells Jesus' story with Moses' shape: a child escaping a murderous king (Matt 2:13-16), forty days in the wilderness, teaching from a mountain, transfigured on a mountain while the Father says, "hear ye him" (Matt 17:5; compare Deut 18:15). Peter names Jesus as the prophet like Moses (Acts 3:22).

Hebrews draws the line that matters: Moses was faithful "as a servant", but Christ "as a son over his own house" (Heb 3:5-6). "The law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). Jesus does not only speak God's word; he is the Son who shows us the Father's face.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/moses-and-christ
blocks.title: James M. Hamilton Jr.
blocks.body: Hamilton discusses Moses as the pattern-setting prophet: Deut 18:15 creates the expectation of a prophet like Moses, later prophets are presented in Mosaic terms, and the pattern reaches its fulfilment in Jesus.

citations.ref: Typology: Understanding the Bible's Promise-Shaped Patterns

blocks.subject: entry:typology/passover-lamb-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: A spotless year-old lamb is killed at twilight, its blood marks the doors, its meat feeds the family, and no bone is broken (Exod 12:5-13, 46). That night God judges Egypt's gods and frees his firstborn son, Israel. (See also the Passover festival and sacrifice entries.)

blocks.subject: entry:typology/passover-lamb-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
John's Gospel opens with "Behold the Lamb of God" (John 1:29) and closes the passion with the Passover detail: "A bone of him shall not be broken" (John 19:36). Paul: "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7).

In Revelation the Lamb "as it had been slain" stands at the centre of the throne and is worthy because he "hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation; and hast made us unto our God kings and priests" (Rev 5:6, 9-10). The Lamb is the victor. The exodus pattern of liberation, now for every nation, is the Christus Victor heart of the type.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/passover-lamb-and-christ
blocks.title: Melito of Sardis
blocks.body: Melito explains typology with the image of a model made before the finished work: the model is precious until the reality comes, then it is set aside. The Passover lamb was such a model; Christ is the reality.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/manna-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: In the wilderness God "rained bread from heaven" (Exod 16:4). Its name comes from the people's question, *man hu*, "What is it?" (16:15). It came each morning, enough for each day, with a double portion before the Sabbath; hoarded manna spoiled (16:16-30). A jar of it was kept before the testimony (16:33). Moses explained its purpose: "that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD" (Deut 8:3).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/manna-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
After feeding the five thousand, Jesus says: "Moses gave you not that bread from heaven; but my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven... I am the bread of life" (John 6:32, 35). Unlike the manna, which the fathers ate and died, this bread gives eternal life (6:49-51).

The manna taught Israel to trust the Father one day at a time; Jesus teaches us to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matt 6:11). The true bread is not a substance but a person, the Son, given by the Father so that we may share his life.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/rock-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body:
At Rephidim God tells Moses, "I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it" (Exod 17:6). Later at Kadesh Moses is told to speak to the rock but strikes it twice in anger, and is barred from entering the land (Num 20:8-12). "The Rock" is also a title for God himself (Deut 32:4, 15, 18).

Paul says Israel "drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4). Later Jewish tradition told of a well that accompanied Israel through the wilderness, which Paul may be echoing.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/rock-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
On the last day of Tabernacles, during the water ceremony, Jesus cries, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink" (John 7:37), speaking of the Spirit. At the cross, "one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water" (John 19:34).

Paul's point is that Christ was already present with Israel, sustaining them in the wilderness. The God who stood upon the rock gives himself as the source of life, and the water is the Spirit poured out from the Son.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/bronze-serpent-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: When fiery serpents bite the complaining Israelites, God tells Moses to make a serpent of bronze and set it on a pole: "every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live" (Num 21:8-9). Centuries later King Hezekiah destroyed it, because the people were burning incense to it and had named it Nehushtan (2 Kgs 18:4).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/bronze-serpent-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
"As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life" (John 3:14-15). Healing came by looking at the very image of what was killing them, lifted up and rendered harmless.

Jesus links his lifting up with victory: "now shall the prince of this world be cast out. And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me" (John 12:31-32). At the cross the power of sin and death is displayed, judged and defeated. Hezekiah's reform is a warning too: the sign points beyond itself to the living God.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/bronze-serpent-and-christ
blocks.title: Justin Martyr
blocks.body: Justin argues that God, who forbade images, commanded the bronze serpent as a sign of the cross: through it God proclaimed salvation for those who believe in the crucified one and the defeat of the serpent who deceived Adam.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/jonah-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: Jonah flees God's call to Nineveh, is thrown into the sea, and is swallowed by a great fish where he stays "three days and three nights" (Jon 1:17) before being vomited onto dry land (2:10). Nineveh repents at his preaching (3:5-10), and the book ends with God's question about his compassion for the city's people and animals (4:11).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/jonah-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
"As Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matt 12:40). In Jewish reckoning any part of a day could count as a day, so Friday to Sunday fits the idiom. "A greater than Jonas is here" (12:41).

The contrast is striking. Jonah ran from God's mercy to the nations and sulked when it came. Jesus goes willingly into death so that the Father's mercy can reach every Nineveh. The sign of Jonah is the resurrection, and its fruit is a worldwide repentance.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/david-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: David is the youngest son, a shepherd, anointed with oil and filled with the Spirit (1 Sam 16:13). He fights Goliath as Israel's single champion, so that his victory becomes the whole people's victory (1 Sam 17). God promises his house an everlasting throne and calls his son God's son (2 Sam 7:12-16). Many of his psalms voice a righteous sufferer who is later vindicated (Ps 22; 69).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/david-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus is greeted as "the Son of David" (Matt 21:9), calls himself the good shepherd (John 10:11), prays the opening of Ps 22 on the cross (Mark 15:34), and is enthroned at the resurrection on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36). He is "the root and the offspring of David" (Rev 22:16).

The Goliath story gives the shape of **Christus Victor**: one champion stands in for his people, defeats the enemy they could not face, and his victory becomes theirs. Christ the King fights for us, wins for us, and shares his kingdom with us.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/david-and-christ
blocks.title: James M. Hamilton Jr.
blocks.body: Hamilton treats the king as one of the major person-types of Scripture: David's life sets a pattern, including suffering before enthronement, that the prophets and psalms develop and that is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David.

citations.ref: Typology: Understanding the Bible's Promise-Shaped Patterns

blocks.subject: entry:typology/melchizedek-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: Melchizedek is both king and priest, which was not allowed in Israel, and he blesses Abraham with bread and wine (Gen 14:18-20). His name means "king of righteousness", and Salem means "peace" (Heb 7:2). Ps 110:4 announces a king who is "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek". (See the Melchizedek christophany entry for the debate over his identity.)

blocks.subject: entry:typology/melchizedek-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Hebrews argues that Christ's priesthood is greater than Levi's: Levi, still "in the loins" of Abraham, paid tithes to Melchizedek (Heb 7:9-10); Jesus' priesthood rests not on genealogy but "the power of an endless life" (7:16); and because he lives for ever, "he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them" (7:25).

He is the King of righteousness and the King of peace, who brings bread and wine and blesses the children of Abraham.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/tabernacle-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body:
"Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them" (Exod 25:8). The tabernacle was built according to a pattern shown to Moses on the mountain (25:9, 40). When it was finished, "the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle" (40:34). Its furnishings, from the gate to the ark, are described in the tabernacle entries.

Hebrews calls the earthly sanctuary "the example and shadow of heavenly things" (Heb 8:5).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/tabernacle-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
"The Word was made flesh, and dwelt [pitched his tent] among us, (and we beheld his glory...)" (John 1:14). What the tabernacle was for Israel, Jesus is in person: the place where God lives with his people and where his glory is seen.

The goal is not a building but a family home: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God" (Rev 21:3).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/tabernacle-and-christ
blocks.title: James M. Hamilton Jr.
blocks.body: Hamilton traces a pattern from creation to tabernacle to temple: Eden is presented as a sanctuary, the tabernacle and temple recall Eden, and the pattern is fulfilled in Christ, in the church as God's temple, and in the new creation.

citations.ref: Typology: Understanding the Bible's Promise-Shaped Patterns

blocks.subject: entry:typology/day-of-atonement-and-christ
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: Once a year the high priest entered the most holy place with blood and incense to cleanse the sanctuary and the people (Lev 16). He wore the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart (Exod 28:9-12, 29), carrying the people with him into God's presence. (See the Day of Atonement festival and two goats entries.)

blocks.subject: entry:typology/day-of-atonement-and-christ
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
"Christ being come an high priest... by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place" (Heb 9:11-12), "into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us" (9:24). He does not go in alone and leave us outside; he goes in as our representative and forerunner (6:20), so that we may "draw near" (10:22).

The high priest carried the names of the tribes on his heart. Christ carries our humanity in himself into the Father's presence. Atonement here means at-one-ment: humanity, in the Son, brought home to the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/day-of-atonement-and-christ
blocks.title: James B. Torrance
blocks.body: James Torrance draws on the Day of Atonement and Hebrews to describe Christ as the one true worshipper and high priest, who bears the names of his people and presents them to the Father, so that our worship is a sharing by the Spirit in his self-offering rather than a performance of our own.

citations.ref: Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace

blocks.subject: entry:typology/exodus-and-new-exodus
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: God brings Israel out of Egypt through the sea, defeats Pharaoh, leads them through the wilderness and dwells among them (Exod 12–15; 40). The prophets use the exodus to describe the return from exile: "Prepare ye the way of the LORD" through the wilderness (Isa 40:3); "Behold, I will do a new thing... I will even make a way in the wilderness" (Isa 43:19).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/exodus-and-new-exodus
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Mark begins with Isaiah's new-exodus voice in the wilderness (Mark 1:2-3). At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about "his decease" (Luke 9:31), literally his *exodos*, which he would accomplish at Jerusalem. Paul says Israel was "baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Cor 10:2), and the victors in Revelation sing "the song of Moses... and the song of the Lamb" (Rev 15:3).

The exodus is the Bible's basic picture of salvation: God defeating the oppressor, freeing his son, and bringing him home. In Christ the enemy is sin and death, and the destination is the Father's presence.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/exodus-and-new-exodus
blocks.title: James M. Hamilton Jr.
blocks.body: Hamilton treats the exodus as one of the key event-types of Scripture: later authors present new acts of deliverance as new exoduses, and the pattern escalates until its fulfilment in Christ's death and resurrection.

citations.ref: Typology: Understanding the Bible's Promise-Shaped Patterns

blocks.subject: entry:typology/exodus-and-new-exodus
blocks.title: N. T. Wright
blocks.body: Wright argues that many Jews of Jesus' day believed the exile was not truly over, and that Jesus understood his ministry and death as bringing about the long-awaited return from exile, the defeat of evil and the return of Israel's God to Zion.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God

blocks.subject: entry:typology/temple-and-body
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: At the dedication of Solomon's temple the glory cloud filled the house (1 Kgs 8:10-11). Ezekiel saw the glory depart before the exile (Ezek 10) and return to a new temple from which a river flows to heal the land (Ezek 43:1-5; 47:1-12). Haggai promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater (Hag 2:9).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/temple-and-body
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
"Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up... But he spake of the temple of his body" (John 2:19, 21). In Jesus the glory has returned and lives among us. After the resurrection, the Spirit makes his people a temple: "know ye not that ye are the temple of God?" (1 Cor 3:16), "an habitation of God through the Spirit" (Eph 2:22).

The temple in Jerusalem fell in AD 70, as Jesus foretold (Mark 13:2). Its purpose was not lost but fulfilled. In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, "for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it" (Rev 21:22).

blocks.subject: entry:typology/temple-and-body
blocks.title: N. T. Wright
blocks.body: Wright argues that Jesus' action in the temple was a prophetic sign of its coming destruction, and that Jesus saw himself and his movement as taking over the temple's role as the place where God meets and forgives his people.

citations.ref: Jesus and the Victory of God

blocks.subject: entry:typology/sabbath-and-rest
blocks.title: The pattern in Scripture
blocks.body: God rests on the seventh day (Gen 2:2-3), and Israel's Sabbath shares that rest (Exod 20:11). The land is also called "the rest" God gives (Deut 12:9), and Joshua brings Israel into it (Josh 21:44). But Ps 95 warns a later generation, "they shall not enter into my rest" (95:11), showing that the promise was not exhausted in Joshua's day.

blocks.subject: entry:typology/sabbath-and-rest
blocks.title: Fulfilment in Christ
blocks.body:
Hebrews argues from Ps 95 that "there remaineth therefore a rest [*sabbatismos*] to the people of God" (Heb 4:9), entered by faith. Jesus offers it in person: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

The rest Christ gives is not idleness but belonging. It is the rest of a child at home with the Father, no longer working to earn a place, sharing God's own delight in his finished work.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/flood-narrative
blocks.title: The structure
blocks.body:
Many commentators have shown that the flood story is told as a *palistrophe*, a long chiasm. The account counts up through periods of seven days, forty days and 150 days as the waters rise, and then counts back down through 150, forty and seven as they recede. The covenant and the list of Noah's sons frame the whole.

At the exact turning point stands Gen 8:1: "And God remembered Noah." In the Bible, God "remembering" is not recall of a forgotten fact but faithful action on behalf of someone (compare Exod 2:24). Scholars who read Genesis as a combination of earlier sources still recognise that the final form has been shaped in this way; the details of the pattern vary between proposals.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/flood-narrative
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
The shape puts the whole story's weight on God's faithfulness. The flood is not the centre; the remembering is. The waters rise to their height, and then God turns everything back toward life.

That is the gospel's pattern too: death rises to its full power, and at the turning point the Father remembers his Son and raises him (Acts 2:24). Peter connects the flood with baptism and the resurrection (1 Pet 3:20-21).

blocks.subject: entry:structure/abraham-cycle
blocks.title: The proposed structure
blocks.body:
A number of scholars have proposed that the Abraham story is arranged as a ring. The clearest correspondences are the framing genealogies (Gen 11:27-32; 22:20-24), the two scenes in which Sarah is taken into a foreign king's house (Gen 12; 20), and the two divine commands with the rare phrase *lech lecha*, "go forth" (Gen 12:1; 22:2), which open and close Abraham's journey of faith.

Proposals differ on the centre. Some put it at the two covenant chapters (Gen 15 and 17), others at the birth of Ishmael between them (Gen 16), and the episodes around Lot and Sodom are grouped differently by different readers. The outline here is one reasonable version.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/abraham-cycle
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
The ring shows that the story is about one question: how will God's promise of a son be fulfilled? At the centre Abraham and Sarah try to secure it themselves through Hagar. The surrounding covenant chapters insist that the son will be God's gift.

The two "go forth" commands frame Abraham's life with trust. In the first he leaves his father; in the last he is willing to give up his son and discovers that God provides. The Father's gift of a son is the heart of the Bible's story.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/leviticus-ring
blocks.title: The proposed structure
blocks.body:
Leviticus sits at the centre of the five books of Moses, and many readers have looked for a symmetrical structure within it. In the outline above, laws of offerings, priests and purity (Lev 1–15) are mirrored by laws of the people's holiness, priests' holiness and holy times (Lev 17–27), with the Day of Atonement (Lev 16) at the centre. Other proposals, including an influential anthropological reading of Leviticus as a ring composition, place the turning point elsewhere, such as Lev 19, and treat chapters 24 and 26–27 differently.

The correspondences are real but loose. Chapter 27 (vows) sits awkwardly after the blessings and curses of chapter 26, and different scholars divide the book in different ways.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/leviticus-ring
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
Whether or not the book is a perfect ring, putting the Day of Atonement and the call to holiness at the centre is theologically apt. The aim of Leviticus is that a holy God can live among a people who are not yet holy: "I will walk among you, and will be your God, and ye shall be my people" (Lev 26:12).

Hebrews reads that centre as fulfilled in Christ's entry into the Father's presence (Heb 9). Holiness in Leviticus flows from God's presence, and in Christ that presence has come to dwell with us.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/psalm-67
blocks.title: The structure
blocks.body:
Ps 67 is a clear example of concentric structure. The identical refrains in verses 3 and 5 frame verse 4, and the prayers for blessing in verses 1-2 and 6-7 frame the whole. The opening echoes the priestly blessing of Num 6:24-26 ("cause his face to shine upon us").

The centre, verse 4, is marked off with *Selah* and speaks of God judging the peoples "righteously" and guiding the nations.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/psalm-67
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
Israel asks to be blessed so that the nations will know God's way. Blessing is never meant to stop with the one who receives it, which is the Abrahamic covenant in miniature (Gen 12:2-3).

At the centre is joy among the nations because God rules justly. God's justice is good news: it is the rule of a Father who sets things right. The psalm is a prayer for the gospel to fill the earth, the hope of a kingdom that grows until "all the ends of the earth shall fear him".

blocks.subject: entry:structure/isaiah-servant-song
blocks.title: The structure
blocks.body:
Most commentators divide Isa 52:13–53:12 into five stanzas of three verses each. The first and last are God's words about the Servant's exaltation; the second and fourth describe his rejection, suffering and death; the central stanza is the confession of "we", the people who misjudged him: "we did esteem him stricken... But he was wounded for our transgressions" (Isa 53:4-5).

The framing words "exalted", "kings" and "the great" (52:13-15; 53:12) mark the movement from humiliation to glory.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/isaiah-servant-song
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
At the centre is not a theory but a confession: we were wrong about him. The people thought the Servant was being punished by God, "smitten of God" (53:4), and then realised that he was bearing *our* sickness and *our* wounds. His suffering was the cost of his solidarity with us, and its result is healing and peace: "the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (53:5).

The shape runs from exaltation to exaltation. The Servant's descent into suffering is the path to victory: "he shall divide the spoil with the strong" (53:12). That is the shape of Phil 2 too.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/amos-5
blocks.title: The structure
blocks.body: Amos 5:1-17 is widely recognised as a carefully built chiasm. A funeral lament (5:1-3) matches the wailing at the end (5:16-17); the calls to "seek... and live" (5:4-6, 14-15) match each other; accusations of perverted justice (5:7, 10-13) surround a short hymn to God the Creator and Judge (5:8-9). The very centre is the line "The LORD is his name" (5:8).

blocks.subject: entry:structure/amos-5
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
At the centre of a passage about corrupt courts and crushed poor people is the name of the LORD. Injustice is not just a social failure; it is a failure to know who God is. The God who turns "the shadow of death into the morning" (5:8) is the God who stands with the poor.

The way out is relational: "Seek ye me, and ye shall live" (5:4), and seeking God means seeking good and establishing "judgment in the gate" (5:15). Biblical justice is restorative: setting the poor back on their feet.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/matthew-13
blocks.title: The proposed structure
blocks.body:
Matthew 13 contains seven or eight parables, often in pairs. Several scholars have suggested a concentric arrangement: the sower, which is about hearing and understanding (13:19, 23), matches the closing question, "Have ye understood all these things?" (13:51); the wheat and tares match the net, both about separation at "the end of the world" (13:40, 49); the mustard seed and leaven match the treasure and the pearl. At the centre stands the fulfilment quotation about parables revealing what was hidden (13:34-35).

This is one proposal among several. The explanations of the sower (13:18-23) and of the tares (13:36-43) and Jesus' move from the crowds to the house (13:36) complicate a neat pattern, and some prefer a structure based on that shift of audience.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/matthew-13
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
The pairs say a great deal about the kingdom. It starts small and grows until it fills everything (mustard seed and leaven), which fits a hopeful, growing view of Christ's reign. It is worth everything (treasure and pearl). And its final sorting belongs to God, not to us (tares and net): the servants are told not to pull up the weeds (13:29-30).

At the centre is revelation: the Father is making known what was hidden, in his Son.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/luke-15
blocks.title: The structure
blocks.body:
Luke frames the chapter with a complaint: the Pharisees and scribes "murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them" (15:2). The chapter ends with the elder brother, who "was angry, and would not go in" to the feast for his returned brother (15:28). He plays the part of the grumblers in the opening scene, and the story is left open: we never learn whether he goes in.

Inside the frame, three parables escalate from one sheep in a hundred, to one coin in ten, to one son in two, each ending with rejoicing and a feast. The refrain "lost... found" recurs (15:6, 9, 24, 32). Detailed inverted structures have also been proposed within the parables themselves (see below); those finer proposals are more debated than the overall frame.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/luke-15
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
The frame tells us who the chapter is for: not only the lost younger son, but the resentful older one. The father goes out to both (15:20, 28). He runs to one and pleads with the other: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine" (15:31).

This is Jesus showing us the Father. God is not a judge waiting for a debt to be paid but a father who runs, embraces, restores the robe, ring and shoes, and throws a feast. Salvation is a homecoming, and the only question left at the end is whether the elder brother will come in.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/philippians-2-hymn
blocks.title: The proposed structure
blocks.body:
The passage has a clear V shape: down from "the form of God" (2:6) through servanthood and death (2:7-8), then up through exaltation (2:9) to universal confession (2:10-11). Many scholars think Paul is quoting or adapting an early Christian hymn, and some see the phrase "even the death of the cross" as Paul's own addition, which breaks the rhythm and so draws attention to itself.

How to divide the lines is disputed: some find two halves (2:6-8 and 2:9-11), others three stanzas or six couplets. The concentric outline here is one proposal.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/philippians-2-hymn
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
The hymn shows what God is like. The Son did not think equality with God was something to exploit; he revealed it by emptying himself and serving. If Jesus is the perfect picture of the Father, then self-giving love is not a departure from divinity but its clearest expression.

The lowest point is the cross, and that is where the turn happens: "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him". The cross is the victory, and the result is a whole creation confessing Jesus as Lord "to the glory of God the Father". Paul's reason for quoting it is relational: "Let this mind be in you" (2:5).

blocks.subject: entry:structure/john-prologue
blocks.title: The proposed structure
blocks.body:
The prologue opens with the Word "with God" (1:1) and closes with the Son "in the bosom of the Father" (1:18), a clear frame. The two notices about John the Baptist (1:6-8, 15) match each other, as do the Light coming to the world (1:9-11) and the Word made flesh (1:14). Several scholars have argued that the centre falls at 1:12-13, the gift of becoming children of God.

Other analyses divide the passage differently, for instance treating it as a series of parallel waves rather than a single chiasm, or placing the centre at 1:14.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/john-prologue
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
If the centre of John's prologue is 1:12-13, then the point of the eternal Word becoming flesh is adoption: "to them gave he power to become the sons of God... born... of God". The Son who has always been in the Father's bosom comes so that we can be children in the Father's house.

The frame says the same thing. No one has seen God, but the only begotten Son, who lives in the Father's embrace, has made him known (1:18). Jesus is the perfect theology: the Father's heart, explained.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/mark-controversies
blocks.title: The proposed structure
blocks.body:
A widely discussed proposal reads Mark 2:1–3:6 as a five-part chiasm. The first and last stories are healings in which Jesus' authority is challenged, inside a building, with the critics' hidden thoughts or watching eyes exposed (2:6-8; 3:2-5). The second and fourth both concern eating (with sinners; plucking grain). The central story is about fasting, where Jesus speaks of himself as the bridegroom who "shall be taken away" (2:20), the first hint of his death in Mark.

Opposition grows across the sequence, from silent questioning (2:6) to a plot to kill him (3:6).

blocks.subject: entry:structure/mark-controversies
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
At the centre is a wedding. Jesus explains why his disciples do not fast: the bridegroom is here. The kingdom he brings is a feast, a joyful union between God and his people, and it cannot be contained in old wineskins.

Around that centre, every conflict is about Jesus restoring people: forgiving and healing, eating with outsiders, feeding the hungry, restoring a withered hand. The religious leaders see a breach of rules; Jesus shows a Father who wants people whole and at the table. The hint of the bridegroom "taken away" shows the cost of that love.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/psalm-8-inclusio
blocks.title: The structure
blocks.body: An *inclusio* (or envelope) repeats the same words at the beginning and end of a unit to frame it. Ps 8 is a textbook example: verses 1 and 9 are identical. Inside the frame the psalm moves from the heavens (8:3) to the question "what is man?" (8:4) and to humanity's crowned role over creation (8:5-8).

blocks.subject: entry:structure/psalm-8-inclusio
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
The frame makes the point: human dignity sits inside God's glory, not in competition with it. Humanity is crowned "with glory and honour" (8:5), but the psalm begins and ends with God's name.

Hebrews reads the psalm through Jesus: "we see not yet all things put under him. But we see Jesus... crowned with glory and honour" (Heb 2:8-9). Christ is the true human who fulfils Ps 8 and brings "many sons unto glory" (Heb 2:10).

blocks.subject: entry:structure/beatitudes-inclusio
blocks.title: The structure
blocks.body: The first and eighth beatitudes end with the same words, "for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matt 5:3, 10), in the present tense, while the six in between have future promises ("shall be comforted", "shall inherit the earth"). This inclusio marks 5:3-10 as a unit; verses 11-12 then turn to address the disciples directly ("Blessed are ye").

blocks.subject: entry:structure/beatitudes-inclusio
blocks.title: Why the shape matters
blocks.body:
The frame says the kingdom belongs to these people now. The blessings in between describe what life in that kingdom looks like and promise its full flowering.

At the heart is a family likeness: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (5:9). The kingdom is the Father's household, and its citizens share his character: merciful, pure-hearted, making peace.

blocks.subject: entry:structure/luke-15
blocks.title: Kenneth E. Bailey
blocks.body: Bailey argues that the parables of Luke 15 are composed with careful Middle Eastern poetic structures, including inverted parallelism, and reads the father's actions, such as running to meet his son, against village culture as a costly, public act of self-humbling love.
